广告商喜欢告诉我们某个产品是“增长最快”或“销量最高”，因为他们无需直接说服我们产品有多好，只需说很多人都这么认为，这似乎就足以证明产品有多好。慈善电视募捐节目的制作人会花费大量时间，不停地列出已经承诺捐款的观众名单。他们传递给那些尚未捐款的人的信息很明确：“看看这么多人决定捐款，这肯定是正确的选择。”在迪斯科热潮鼎盛时期，一些迪斯科舞厅老板为了证明舞厅的品质，故意制造出一种“看得见的社会认同感”，明明里面空间充足，却在外面排起了长队。销售人员也被教导要用大量顾客购买产品的案例来增强推销效果。销售和激励顾问卡维特·罗伯特在给销售培训生的建议中很好地概括了这一原则：“由于 95% 的人是模仿者，只有 5% 的人是发起者，因此人们更容易被他人的行为所说服，而不是被我们能提供的任何证据所说服。”

Researchers, too, have employed procedures based on the principle of social proof—sometimes with astounding results. One psychologist in particular, Albert Bandura, has led the way in developing such procedures for the elimination of undesirable behavior. Bandura and his colleagues have shown how people suffering from phobias can be rid of these extreme fears in an amazingly simple fashion. For instance, in an early study nursery-school-age children chosen because they were terrified of dogs merely watched a little boy playing happily with a dog for twenty minutes a day. This exhibition produced such marked changes in the reactions of the fearful children that after only four days, 67 percent of them were willing to climb into a playpen with a dog and remain confined there, petting and scratching it while everyone else left the room. Moreover, when the researchers tested the children's fear levels again one month later, they found that the improvement had not evaporated during that time; in fact, the children were more willing than ever to interact with dogs.

研究人员也运用了基于社会认同原理的方法，有时取得了惊人的成果。其中一位心理学家阿尔伯特·班杜拉尤其在开发此类消除不良行为的方法方面做出了开创性贡献。班杜拉和他的同事们展示了如何以一种极其简单的方式帮助恐惧症患者摆脱这些极端的恐惧。例如，在一项早期研究中，研究人员挑选了一些因为害怕狗而被选中的幼儿园儿童，让他们每天观看一个小男孩和一只狗快乐地玩耍20分钟。这种观察显著改变了这些恐惧儿童的反应，仅仅四天后，67%的儿童就愿意爬进一个有狗的围栏里，待在里面抚摸和挠痒，而其他人则离开房间。此外，当研究人员在一个月后再次测试这些儿童的恐惧程度时，他们发现这种改善并没有消失；事实上，孩子们比以往任何时候都更愿意与狗互动。

An important practical discovery was made in a second study of children who were exceptionally afraid of dogs: To reduce their fears, it was not necessary to provide live demonstrations of another child playing with a dog; film clips had the same effect. And the most effective type of clips were those depicting not one but a variety of other children interacting with their dogs; apparently the principle of social proof works best when the proof is provided by the actions of a lot of other people. 3

在第二项针对极度害怕狗的儿童的研究中，一项重要的实践发现是：为了减轻他们的恐惧，无需提供其他孩子与狗玩耍的现场演示；视频片段也能达到同样的效果。而且，最有效的视频片段是那些展现多个孩子与他们的狗互动的片段；显然，当社会认同原则由许多人的行为提供证据时，它的效果最佳。

The powerful influence of filmed examples in changing the behavior of children can be used as therapy for various problems. Some striking evidence is available in the research of psychologist Robert O'Connor on socially withdrawn preschool children. We have all seen children of this sort, terribly shy, standing alone at the fringes of the games and groupings of their peers. O'Connor worried that a long-term pattern of isolation was forming, even at an early age, that would create persistent difficulties in social comfort and adjustment through adulthood. In an attempt to reverse the pattern, O'Connor made a film containing eleven different scenes in a nursery-school setting. Each scene began by showing a different solitary child watching some ongoing social activity and then actively joining the activity, to everyone's enjoyment. O'Connor selected a group of the most severely withdrawn children from four preschools and showed them his film. The impact was impressive. The isolates immediately began to interact with their peers at a level equal to that of the normal children in the schools. Even more astonishing was what O'Connor found when he returned to observe six weeks later. While the withdrawn children who had not seen O'Connor's film remained as isolated as ever, those who had viewed it were now leading their schools in amount of social activity. It seems that this twenty-three-minute movie, viewed just once, was enough to reverse a potential pattern of lifelong maladaptive behavior. Such is the potency of the principle of social proof.

影像案例对改变儿童行为的强大影响力可以用于治疗各种问题。心理学家罗伯特·奥康纳对社交退缩的学龄前儿童的研究提供了令人瞩目的证据。我们都见过这样的孩子：他们极其害羞，总是独自站在同伴游戏和群体活动的边缘。奥康纳担心，这种长期的孤立模式，即使在幼儿时期就已经形成，并会在成年后造成持续的社交困难和适应障碍。为了扭转这种局面，奥康纳拍摄了一部包含11个不同场景的影片，拍摄地点设在幼儿园。每个场景都以一个孤僻的孩子观察正在进行的社交活动开始，然后积极地加入其中，让大家都感到开心。奥康纳从四所幼儿园中挑选了一组社交退缩最严重的孩子，并给他们播放了这部影片。影片的效果令人印象深刻。这些孤僻的孩子立刻开始与同伴互动，其互动水平与学校里其他正常的孩子不相上下。更令人惊讶的是，奥康纳六周后再次观察时发现的情况。那些没有看过奥康纳影片的内向孩子依然孤僻，而看过影片的孩子在社交活动方面却名列前茅。这部时长仅23分钟的影片，只需观看一次，就足以扭转一种可能伴随终生的适应不良行为模式。这就是社会认同原则的强大力量。

When it comes to illustrations of the strength of social proof, there is one that is far and away my favorite. Several features account for its appeal: It offers a superb example of the much underused method of participant observation, in which a scientist studies a process by becoming immersed in its natural occurrence; it provides information of interest to such diverse groups as historians, psychologists, and theologians; and, most important, it shows how social evidence can be used on us—not by others, but by ourselves—to assure us that what we prefer to be true will seem to be true.

说到社会认同的力量，我最喜欢的例子莫过于此。它之所以吸引人，有几个原因：首先，它完美地诠释了参与式观察法——一种常被忽视的研究方法，即科学家通过沉浸于自然发生的事件中来研究某个过程；其次，它为历史学家、心理学家和神学家等不同领域的学者提供了有价值的信息；最后，也是最重要的一点，它揭示了社会认同如何作用于我们自身——不是被他人利用，而是被我们自己利用——来确保我们倾向于相信的事情看起来就是真的。

The story is an old one, requiring an examination of ancient data, for the past is dotted with millennial religious movements. Various sects and cults have prophesied that on one or another particular date there would arrive a period of redemption and great happiness for those who believed in the group's teachings. In each instance it has been predicted that the beginning of the time of salvation would be marked by an important and undeniable event, usually the cataclysmic end of the world.

这个故事由来已久，需要考证古代史料，因为历史上曾出现过许多延续千年的宗教运动。各种教派和团体都预言，在某个特定的日期，信奉其教义的人将会迎来救赎和极乐的时代。在每一种预言中，救赎时代的开始都将以一件重大且无可辩驳的事件为标志，通常是世界末日的灾难性灾难。

Of course, these predictions have invariably proved false. To the acute dismay of the members of such groups, the end has never appeared as scheduled.

当然，这些预测无一例外都被证明是错误的。令这些群体成员深感失望的是，结局从未如期而至。

But immediately following the obvious failure of the prophecy, history records an enigmatic pattern. Rather than disbanding in disillusion, the cultists often become strengthened in their convictions. Risking the ridicule of the populace, they take to the streets, publicly asserting their dogma and seeking converts with a fervor that is intensified, not diminished, by the clear disconfirmation of a central belief. So it was with the Montanists of second-century Turkey, with the Anabaptists of sixteenth-century Holland, with the Sabbataists of seventeenth-century Izmir, with the Millerites of nineteenth-century America. And, thought a trio of interested social scientists, so it might be with a doomsday cult based in modern-day Chicago. The scientists—Leon Festinger, Henry Riecken, and Stanley Schachter—who were then colleagues at the University of Minnesota, heard about the Chicago group and felt it worthy of close study. Their decision to investigate by joining the group, incognito, as new believers and by placing additional paid observers among its ranks resulted in a remarkably rich firsthand account of the goings-on before and after the day of predicted catastrophe. 5

然而，在预言明显落空之后，历史却记录了一种令人费解的模式。这些邪教徒非但没有因幻灭而解散，反而往往更加坚定了自己的信念。他们不顾民众的嘲笑，走上街头，公开宣扬自己的教条，并以一种非但没有减弱，反而因核心信仰的彻底破灭而愈发狂热地寻求皈依者。公元二世纪土耳其的蒙坦派、十六世纪荷兰的再洗礼派、十七世纪伊兹密尔的萨巴泰派、十九世纪美国的米勒派，都曾如此。三位感兴趣的社会科学家认为，一个以现代芝加哥为据点的末日邪教也可能如此。这三位科学家——莱昂·费斯廷格、亨利·里肯和斯坦利·沙赫特——当时是明尼苏达大学的同事，他们听说了这个芝加哥团体，并认为它值得深入研究。他们决定以新信徒的身份秘密加入该组织进行调查，并在其成员中安插付费观察员，最终获得了关于预言灾难发生前后情况的极其丰富的第一手资料。

The cult of believers was small, never numbering more than thirty members. Its leaders were a middle-aged man and woman, whom the researchers renamed, for purposes of publication, Dr. Thomas Armstrong and Mrs. Marian Keech. Dr. Armstrong, a physician on the staff of a college student health service, had a long-held interest in mysticism, the occult, and flying saucers; as such he served as a respected authority on these subjects for the group. Mrs. Keech, though, was the center of attention and activity. Earlier in the year she had begun to receive messages from spiritual beings, whom she called the Guardians, located on other planets. It was these messages, flowing through Marian Keech's hand via the device of "automatic writing," that were to form the bulk of the cult's religious belief system. The teachings of the Guardians were loosely linked to traditional Christian thought. No wonder that one of the Guardians, Sananda, eventually "revealed" himself as the current embodiment of Jesus.

这个信徒团体规模很小，成员从未超过三十人。其领导者是一对中年夫妇，为了便于发表，研究人员将他们分别改名为托马斯·阿姆斯特朗博士和玛丽安·基奇夫人。阿姆斯特朗博士是大学学生健康服务中心的医生，长期以来对神秘主义、玄学和飞碟颇感兴趣；因此，他是该团体中这些领域的权威。然而，基奇夫人才是团体的中心人物。年初，她开始接收到来自其他星球的灵体的信息，她称这些灵体为“守护者”。这些信息通过玛丽安·基奇的“自动书写”装置传递出来，构成了该团体宗教信仰体系的主体。守护者的教义与传统的基督教思想有着松散的联系。难怪其中一位守护者萨南达最终“显灵”，自称是耶稣的化身。

The transmissions from the Guardians, always the subjects of much discussion and interpretation among the group, gained new significance when they began to foretell a great impending disaster—a flood that would begin in the Western Hemisphere and eventually engulf the world. Although the cultists were understandably alarmed at first, further messages assured them that they and all those who believed in the Lessons sent through Mrs. Keech would survive. Before the calamity, spacemen were to arrive and carry off the believers in flying saucers to a place of safety, presumably on another planet. Very little detail was provided about the rescue except that the believers were to make themselves ready for pickup by rehearsing certain passwords to be exchanged ("I left my hat at home." "What is your question?" "I am my own porter.") and by removing all metal from their clothes—because the wearing or carrying of metal made saucer travel "extremely dangerous."

来自守护者的讯息一直是信徒们热议和解读的话题，而当它们开始预言一场即将到来的巨大灾难——一场始于西半球并最终席卷全球的洪水——时，这些讯息的意义更是与日俱增。尽管信徒们起初惊恐万分，但随后的讯息让他们确信，他们以及所有相信基奇夫人所传达的教诲的人都将幸存下来。灾难发生前，宇航员将抵达，用飞碟将信徒们转移到一个安全的地方，大概是在另一个星球上。关于救援的细节很少，只提到信徒们需要做好准备，比如练习一些交换口令（“我把帽子落在家里了。”“你的问题是什么？”“我自己就是搬运工。”），以及脱掉衣服上的所有金属——因为佩戴或携带金属会使飞碟旅行“极其危险”。

As Festinger, Riecken, and Schachter observed the preparations during the weeks prior to the flood date, they noted with special interest two significant aspects of the members' behavior. First, the level of commitment to the cult's belief system was very high. In anticipation of their departure from doomed Earth, irrevocable steps were taken by the group members. Most had incurred the opposition of family and friends to their beliefs but had persisted nonetheless in their convictions, often when it meant losing the affections of these others. In fact, several of the members were threatened by neighbors or family with legal actions designed to have them declared insane. In Dr. Armstrong's case, a motion was filed by his sister to have his two younger children taken away. Many believers quit their jobs or neglected their studies to devote full time to the movement. Some even gave or threw away their personal belongings, expecting them shortly to be of no use. These were people whose certainty that they had the truth allowed them to withstand enormous social, economic, and legal pressures and whose commitment to their dogma grew as each pressure was resisted.

在洪水来临前的几周里，费斯廷格、里肯和沙赫特观察着准备工作，他们特别关注到成员们行为的两个显著特点。首先，他们对邪教信仰体系的忠诚度极高。为了迎接即将毁灭的地球，这些成员采取了不可逆转的行动。他们中的大多数人都因为自己的信仰而遭到家人和朋友的反对，但他们仍然坚持己见，即便这意味着失去这些人的关爱。事实上，一些成员甚至受到邻居或家人的威胁，他们扬言要通过法律手段将他们定性为精神失常。以阿姆斯特朗博士为例，他的妹妹甚至提出动议，要求带走他的两个年幼的孩子。许多信徒辞去了工作或荒废了学业，全身心投入到这个运动中。有些人甚至将自己的个人物品赠送或丢弃，因为他们预料到这些东西很快就会变得毫无用处。这些人坚信自己掌握了真理，因此能够承受巨大的社会、经济和法律压力，并且随着每一次压力的抵挡，他们对自身教条的忠诚度也越来越高。

The second significant aspect of the believers' preflood actions was a curious form of inaction. For individuals so clearly convinced of the validity of their creed, they did surprisingly little to spread the word. Although they did initially make public the news of the coming disaster, there was no attempt to seek converts, to proselyte actively. They were willing to sound the alarm and to counsel those who voluntarily responded to it, but that was all.

信徒们在洪水前行为的第二个重要方面是一种奇特的无所作为。尽管他们如此确信自己信仰的正确性，却出人意料地很少传播福音。虽然他们最初确实公开了即将到来的灾难的消息，但并没有试图寻找皈依者，也没有积极地劝人改信。他们愿意发出警报，并为那些自愿回应的人提供劝导，仅此而已。

The group's distaste for recruitment efforts was evident in various ways besides the lack of personal persuasion attempts. Secrecy was maintained in many matters—extra copies of the Lessons were burned, passwords and secret signs were instituted, the contents of certain private tape recordings were not to be discussed with outsiders (so secret were the tapes that even longtime believers were prohibited from taking notes of them). Publicity was avoided. As the day of disaster approached, increasing numbers of newspaper, television, and radio reporters converged on the group's headquarters in the Keech house. For the most part, these people were turned away or ignored. The most frequent answer to their questions was, "No comment." Although discouraged for a time, the media representatives returned with a ven-geance when Dr. Armstrong's religious activities caused him to be fired from his post on the college health service staff; one especially persistent newsman had to be threatened with a lawsuit. A similar siege was repelled on the eve of the flood when a swarm of reporters pushed and pestered the believers for information. Afterward, the researchers summarized the group's preflood stance on public exposure and recruitment in respectful tones: "Exposed to a tremendous burst of publicity, they had made every attempt to dodge fame; given dozens of opportunities to proselyte, they had remained evasive and secretive and behaved with an almost superior indifference."

除了不进行个人劝说之外，该组织对招募工作的厌恶还体现在方方面面。许多事情都严格保密——多余的《教义》副本会被烧毁，组织会制定口令和暗号，某些私人录音带的内容不得与外人讨论（这些录音带的保密程度之高，甚至连长期信徒都被禁止做笔记）。他们刻意避免公开露面。随着灾难发生日期的临近，越来越多的报纸、电视和广播记者涌向位于基奇住宅的组织总部。但大多数情况下，这些人要么被拒之门外，要么被置之不理。他们最常听到的回答是“无可奉告”。尽管一度感到沮丧，但当阿姆斯特朗博士的宗教活动导致他被大学卫生服务部门解雇后，媒体记者们又卷土重来，而且来势汹汹；其中一位特别执着的记者甚至被威胁要提起诉讼。在洪水来临前夕，一群记者蜂拥而至，围堵信徒，试图获取信息，但最终被击退。事后，研究人员以尊重的语气总结了该群体在洪水前对公众曝光和招募的态度：“面对铺天盖地的媒体曝光，他们竭力避免成名；尽管有数十次机会可以传教，他们却始终闪烁其词、秘而不宣，表现得近乎高高在上、漠不关心。”

Eventually, when all the reporters and would-be converts had been cleared from the house, the believers began making their final preparations for the arrival of the spaceship scheduled for midnight that night. The scene, as viewed by Festinger, Riecken, and Schachter, must have seemed like absurdist theater. Otherwise ordinary people—housewives, college students, a high-school boy, a publisher, an M.D., a hardwarestore clerk and his mother—were participating earnestly in tragic comedy. They took direction from a pair of members who were periodically in touch with the Guardians; Marian Keech's written messages from Sananda were being supplemented that evening by "the Bertha," a former beautician through whose tongue the "Creator" gave instruction. They rehearsed their lines diligently, calling out in chorus the responses to be made before entering the rescue saucer, "I am my own porter." "I am my own pointer." They discussed seriously whether the message from a caller identifying himself as Captain Video—a TV space character of the time—was properly interpreted as a prank or a coded communication from their rescuers. And they performed in costume. In keeping with the admonition to carry nothing metallic aboard the saucer, the believers wore clothing that had been cut open to allow the metal pieces to be torn out. The metal eyelets in their shoes had been ripped away. The women were braless or wore brassieres whose metal stays had been removed. The men had yanked the zippers out of their pants, which were supported by lengths of rope in place of belts.

最终，当所有记者和潜在的皈依者都被请出屋子后，信徒们开始为当晚午夜到来的宇宙飞船做最后的准备。在费斯廷格、里肯和沙赫特看来，这场景一定像是一出荒诞剧。原本平凡的人们——家庭主妇、大学生、高中生、出版商、医生、五金店店员和他的母亲——正认真地参与着这出悲喜剧。他们听从两位定期与守护者联系的成员的指示；当晚，玛丽安·基奇从萨南达发出的书面信息得到了“伯莎”的补充，这位前美容师通过“造物主”的口吻传达指示。他们认真地排练着台词，齐声喊出进入救援飞碟前要说的话：“我是我自己的搬运工。”“我是我自己的指示者。”他们认真讨论着，一个自称“视频队长”（当时电视上的太空角色）的来电究竟是恶作剧，还是救援人员发出的暗号。他们还穿上了戏服。为了遵守“飞碟上不携带任何金属物品”的警告，这些信徒们穿着被剪开的衣服，以便把金属部件扯出来。他们鞋子上的金属鞋眼也被扯掉了。女人们要么没穿胸罩，要么穿的胸罩里的金属支撑也被拆掉了。男人们则把裤子的拉链扯掉了，裤子用绳子代替腰带固定。

The group's fanaticism concerning the removal of all metal was vividly experienced by one of the researchers who remarked, twenty-five minutes before midnight, that he had forgotten to extract the zipper from his trousers. As the observers tell it, "this knowledge produced a near panic reaction. He was rushed into the bedroom where Dr. Armstrong, his hands trembling and his eyes darting to the clock every few seconds, slashed out the zipper with a razor blade and wrenched its clasps free with wire-cutters." The hurried operation finished, the researcher was returned to the living room a slightly less metallic but, one supposes, much paler man.

该组织对去除所有金属的狂热程度，一位研究人员对此深有体会。午夜前25分钟，他突然发现自己忘了把裤子拉链取下来。据旁观者描述，“他意识到这一点后几乎惊慌失措。他被匆匆带进卧室，阿姆斯特朗博士双手颤抖，眼睛每隔几秒就瞥一眼时钟，用剃须刀片割开拉链，然后用钢丝钳剪断拉链扣。” 匆忙完成之后，这位研究人员被送回客厅，虽然身上的金属味少了一些，但脸色想必也苍白了许多。

As the time appointed for their departure grew very close, the believers settled into a lull of soundless anticipation. With trained scientists on site, we are afforded a detailed account of the events that transpired during this momentous period in the life of the group:

随着出发时间的临近，信徒们陷入了寂静的期待之中。由于有训练有素的科学家在现场，我们得以详细了解这个群体生命中这一重要时期所发生的事件：

The last ten minutes were tense ones for the group in the living room. They had nothing to do but sit and wait, their coats in their laps. In the tense silence two clocks ticked loudly, one about ten minutes faster than the other. When the faster of the two pointed to twelve-five, one of the observers remarked aloud on the fact. A chorus of people replied that midnight had not yet come. Bob Eastman affirmed that the slower clock was correct; he had set it himself only that afternoon. It showed only four minutes before midnight.
客厅里的最后十分钟，对这群人来说无比煎熬。他们只能坐在那里等待，外套搭在腿上。在令人窒息的寂静中，两座钟滴答作响，一座比另一座快了大约十分钟。当快的那座钟指向十二点五分时，其中一位观察者脱口而出。众人齐声回应说，午夜还没到。鲍勃·伊斯特曼断言，慢的那座钟走得准；那是他当天下午才调的。它显示离午夜还有四分钟。
These four minutes passed in complete silence except for a single utterance. When the [slower] clock on the mantel showed only one minute remaining before the guide to the saucer was due, Marian exclaimed in a strained, high-pitched voice: "And not a plan has gone astray!" The clock chimed twelve, each stroke painfully clear in the expectant hush. The believers sat motionless.
这四分钟在一片寂静中过去，只有一声轻响。壁炉架上的慢钟显示，距离碟子向导到达只剩一分钟时，玛丽安用一种紧张而尖锐的声音喊道：“计划万无一失！”钟声敲响了十二下，在屏息凝神的寂静中，每一次敲击都显得格外清晰。信徒们一动不动地坐着。
One might have expected some visible reaction. Midnight had passed and nothing had happened. The cataclysm itself was less than seven hours away. But there was little to see in the reactions of the people in that room. There was no talking, no sound. People sat stock-still, their faces seemingly frozen and expressionless. Mark Post was the only person who even moved. He lay down on the sofa and closed his eyes but did not sleep. Later, when spoken to, he answered monosyllabically but otherwise lay immobile. The others showed nothing on the surface, although it became clear later that they had been hit hard.
人们或许会期待一些明显的反应。午夜已过，却什么也没发生。灾难本身还有不到七个小时就要降临。但房间里人们的反应却几乎毫无生气。没有说话，没有声音。人们一动不动地坐着，脸上的表情仿佛凝固了一般，毫无表情。只有马克·波斯特动了一下。他躺在沙发上，闭上眼睛，却没有睡着。后来，当有人和他说话时，他只是单音节地回答，除此之外，他一动不动。其他人表面上没有任何表情，尽管后来人们才明白，他们都受到了重创。
Gradually, painfully, an atmosphere of despair and confusion settled over the group. They reexamined the prediction and the accompanying messages. Dr. Armstrong and Mrs. Keech reiterated their faith. The believers mulled over their predicament and discarded explanation after explanation as unsatisfactory. At one point, toward 4 A.M., Mrs. Keech broke down and cried bitterly. She knew, she sobbed, that there were some who were beginning to doubt but that the group must beam light to those who needed it most and that the group must hold together. The rest of the believers were losing their composure, too. They were all visibly shaken and many were close to tears. It was now almost 4:30 A.M., and still no way of handling the disconfirmation had been found. By now, too, most of the group were talking openly about the failure of the escort to come at midnight. The group seemed near dissolution.
渐渐地，绝望和迷茫的气氛痛苦地笼罩着整个团体。他们重新审视了预言和随之而来的信息。阿姆斯特朗博士和基奇夫人重申了他们的信仰。信徒们反复思量着眼前的困境，并逐一否定了各种解释。凌晨四点左右，基奇夫人崩溃了，痛哭流涕。她抽泣着说，她知道有些人开始怀疑，但团体必须为最需要帮助的人带来光明，团体必须团结一致。其他信徒也开始失去冷静。他们都明显受到了惊吓，许多人眼眶含泪。此时已近凌晨四点半，他们仍然找不到应对预言落空的方法。与此同时，团体中的大多数人也开始公开谈论午夜时分护送人员未能出现的事情。团体似乎濒临解散。

In the midst of this gathering doubt, as cracks crawled through the believers' confidence, the researchers witnessed a pair of remarkable incidents, one after another. The first occurred at about 4:45 A.M., when Marian Keech's hand suddenly leapt to the task of transcribing through "automatic writing" the text of a holy message from above. When read aloud, the communication proved to be an elegant explanation for the events of that night. "The little group, sitting alone all night long, had spread so much light that God had saved the world from destruction." Although neat and efficient, this explanation was not wholly satisfying by itself; for example, after hearing it, one member simply rose, put on his hat and coat, and left. Something additional was needed to restore the believers to their previous levels of faith.

在疑虑渐生、信徒信心开始动摇之际，研究人员目睹了两件非同寻常的事件，而且接连发生。第一件发生在凌晨4点45分左右，玛丽安·基奇的手突然开始“自动书写”，抄录了来自上天的神圣讯息。当这段讯息被朗读出来时，它巧妙地解释了当晚发生的一切：“这个小团体整夜静坐，散发了如此耀眼的光芒，以至于上帝拯救了世界免于毁灭。”尽管这个解释简洁明了，但却并不完全令人满意；例如，一位信徒在听完之后，只是起身戴上帽子，穿上外套，便离开了。要想让信徒们重拾信心，还需要一些其他的解释。

It was at this point that the second notable incident occurred to meet that need. Once again, the words of those who were present offer a vivid description:

正是在这个时候，为了满足这一需求，发生了第二件引人注目的事件。在场者的描述再次生动形象：

The atmosphere in the group changed abruptly and so did their behavior. Within minutes after she had read the message explaining the disconfirmation, Mrs. Keech received another message instructing her to publicize the explanation. She reached for the telephone and began dialing the number of a newspaper. While she was waiting to be connected, someone asked: "Marian, is this the first time you have called the newspaper yourself?" Her reply was immediate: "Oh, yes, this is the first time I have ever called them. I have never had anything to tell them before, but now I feel it is urgent." The whole group could have echoed her feelings, for they all felt a sense of urgency. As soon as Marian had finished her call, the other members took turns telephoning newspapers, wire services, radio stations, and national magazines to spread the explanation of the failure of the flood. In their desire to spread the word quickly and resoundingly, the believers now opened for public attention matters that had been thus far utterly secret. Where only hours earlier they had shunned newspaper reporters and felt that the attention they were getting in the press was painful, they now became avid seekers for publicity.
小组的气氛骤然改变，成员们的行为也随之改变。基奇太太读完解释预言落空的讯息后几分钟，就收到了另一条讯息，指示她将这一解释公之于众。她拿起电话，开始拨打报社的号码。在等待接通的过程中，有人问道：“玛丽安，这是你第一次亲自打电话给报社吗？”她立刻回答：“哦，是的，这是我第一次打电话给他们。我以前从未告诉过他们什么，但现在我觉得事情很紧急。”整个小组似乎都感同身受，因为他们都感到事态紧急。玛丽安挂断电话后，其他成员轮流打电话给报社、通讯社、广播电台和全国性杂志，传播洪水预言落空的解释。为了迅速而响亮地传播消息，这些信徒们现在将此前完全保密的事情公之于众。就在几个小时前，他们还对报社记者避之不及，觉得媒体的关注令他们痛苦不堪，而现在他们却成了热衷于出名的人。

Not only had the long-standing policies concerning secrecy and publicity done an about-face, so, too, had the group's attitude toward potential converts. Whereas likely recruits who previously visited the house had been mostly ignored, turned away, or treated with casual attention, the day following the disconfirmation saw a different story.

不仅长期以来关于保密和公开的政策发生了180度大转弯，该组织对待潜在皈依者的态度也截然不同。此前，那些可能被招募的人大多被忽视、拒之门外或被敷衍对待，但在声明被否认后的第二天，情况却截然不同。

All callers were admitted, all questions were answered, attempts were made to proselyte all such visitors. The members' unprecedented willingness to accommodate possible new recruits was perhaps best demonstrated when nine high-school students arrived on the following night to speak with Mrs. Keech.

所有来电者都被允许进入，所有问题都得到了解答，并且他们试图劝说所有来访者加入他们的组织。成员们空前热情地接纳潜在新成员，这一点或许在第二天晚上九名高中生前来与基奇夫人交谈时体现得最为淋漓尽致。

They found her at the telephone deep in a discussion of flying saucers with a caller whom, it later turned out, she believed to be a spaceman. Eager to continue talking to him and at the same time anxious to keep her new guests, Marian simply included them in the conversation and, for more than an hour, chatted alternately with her guests in the living room and the "spaceman" on the other end of the telephone. So intent was she on proselyting that she seemed unable to let any opportunity go by.
他们发现她正坐在电话旁，和一个后来才知道她认为是宇航员的人热烈地讨论着飞碟。玛丽安既想继续和他聊天，又急于留住新来的客人，于是干脆把他们也拉进了谈话中。接下来的一个多小时里，她一会儿和客厅里的客人聊天，一会儿又和电话那头的“宇航员”聊天。她如此热衷于传教，似乎不放过任何机会。

To what can we attribute the believers' radical turnabout? In the space of a few hours, they went from clannish and taciturn hoarders of the Word to expansive and eager disseminators of it. And what could have possessed them to choose such an ill-timed instant—when the failure of the flood was likely to cause nonbelievers to view the group and its dogma as laughable?

信徒们的这种彻底转变究竟源于何处？短短几个小时内，他们就从封闭寡言、固守教义的群体，变成了热情洋溢、积极传播教义的先锋。而他们又为何偏偏选择在这样一个不合时宜的时刻——洪水灾害的失败很可能会让非信徒们将他们及其教义视为笑柄？

The crucial event occurred sometime during "the night of the flood," when it became increasingly clear that the prophecy would not be fulfilled. Oddly, it was not their prior certainty that drove the members to propagate the faith; it was an encroaching sense of uncertainty. It was the dawning realization that if the spaceship and flood predictions were wrong, so might be the entire belief system on which they rested. For those huddled in the Keech living room, that growing possibility must have seemed hideous.

关键事件发生在“洪水之夜”的某个时刻，当时人们越来越清楚地意识到，预言不会实现。奇怪的是，驱使信徒们传播信仰的并非他们先前的笃定，而是一种日益加剧的不确定感。他们逐渐意识到，如果关于宇宙飞船和洪水的预言是错误的，那么他们赖以生存的整个信仰体系也可能是错误的。对于挤在基奇家客厅里的那些人来说，这种日益增长的可能性无疑是可怕的。

The group members had gone too far, given up too much for their beliefs to see them destroyed; the shame, the economic cost, the mockery would be too great to bear. The overarching need of the cultists to cling to those beliefs seeps poignantly from their own words: From a young woman with a three-year-old child:

这些信徒已经走得太远，为了信仰付出了太多，他们无法承受信仰崩塌的打击；耻辱、经济损失和嘲笑都让他们难以承受。这些邪教徒对信仰的执着，从他们自己的话语中，无不令人心酸地流露出来：一位带着三岁孩子的年轻女子说道：

I have to believe the flood is coming on the twenty-first because I've spent all my money. I quit my job, I quit computer school.... I have to believe.
我必须相信洪水会在21号到来，因为我已经花光了所有的钱。我辞掉了工作，也退学了……我必须相信。

And from Dr. Armstrong to one of the researchers four hours after the failure of the saucermen to arrive:

在飞碟宇航员未能抵达目的地四个小时后，阿姆斯特朗博士给其中一位研究人员说：

I've had to go a long way. I've given up just about everything. I've cut every tie. I've burned every bridge. I've turned my back on the world. I can't afford to doubt. I have to believe. And there isn't any other truth.
我走了很远的路。我几乎放弃了一切。我断绝了所有关系。我毁掉了所有桥梁。我背弃了这个世界。我不能再怀疑了。我必须相信。除此之外，别无他法。

Imagine the corner in which Dr. Armstrong and his followers found themselves as morning approached. So massive was the commitment to their beliefs that no other truth was tolerable. Yet that set of beliefs had just taken a merciless pounding from physical reality: No saucer had landed, no spacemen had knocked, no flood had come, nothing had happened as prophesied. Since the only acceptable form of truth had been undercut by physical proof, there was but one way out of the corner for the group. They had to establish another type of proof for the validity of their beliefs: social proof.

想象一下，当黎明临近时，阿姆斯特朗博士和他的追随者们身处何种困境。他们对自己的信仰如此笃信，以至于任何其他真相都无法容忍。然而，这套信仰刚刚遭受了来自物理现实的无情打击：没有飞碟着陆，没有宇航员敲门，没有洪水泛滥，预言中的一切都没有发生。既然唯一可接受的真理已被物理证据推翻，那么他们只有一条出路。他们必须为自己的信仰找到另一种证明：社会认同。

This, then, explains their sudden shift from secretive conspirators to zealous missionaries. And it explains the curious timing of the shift—precisely when a direct disconfirmation of their beliefs had rendered them least convincing to outsiders. It was necessary to risk the scorn and derision of the nonbelievers because publicity and recruitment efforts provided the only remaining hope. If they could spread the Word, if they could inform the uninformed, if they could persuade the skeptics, and if, by so doing, they could win new converts, their threatened but treasured beliefs would become truer. The principle of social proof says so: The greater the number of people who find any idea correct, the more the idea will be correct. The group's assignment was clear; since the physical evidence could not be changed, the social evidence had to be. Convince and ye shall be convinced! 6

这就解释了他们为何突然从秘密的阴谋家转变为狂热的传教士。这也解释了这种转变的时机为何如此奇特——恰恰是在他们的信仰遭到直接否定，以至于外界对他们的说服力最弱的时候。他们不得不冒着被非信徒嘲笑和讥讽的风险，因为宣传和招募是他们仅存的希望。如果他们能够传播福音，如果他们能够让不知情的人了解真相，如果他们能够说服怀疑论者，并且通过这种方式赢得新的信徒，那么他们那些岌岌可危却又无比珍视的信仰就会变得更加真实。社会认同原则正是如此：认为某个观点正确的人越多，这个观点就越正确。这个团体的任务很明确：既然物质证据无法改变，那就只能改变社会证据。“说服别人，你们就会被说服！”

CAUSE OF DEATH: UNCERTAIN(TY)

死因：不明

All the weapons of influence discussed in this book work better under some conditions than under others. If we are to defend ourselves adequately against any such weapon, it is vital that we know its optimal operating conditions in order to recognize when we are most vulnerable to its influence. In the case of the principle of social proof, we have already had a hint of one time when it works best. Among the Chicago believers, it was a sense of shaken confidence that triggered their craving for converts. In general, when we are unsure of ourselves, when the situation is unclear or ambiguous, when uncertainty reigns, we are most likely to look to and accept the actions of others as correct.

本书讨论的所有影响力手段，在某些情况下比其他情况下更有效。如果我们想要有效地抵御任何此类手段，就必须了解其最佳运作条件，以便识别我们何时最容易受到其影响。就社会认同原则而言，我们已经略知一二它在何种情况下最为有效。在芝加哥信徒群体中，正是信心的动摇激发了他们渴望发展新信徒的热情。总的来说，当我们对自己缺乏信心，当情况不明朗或模糊不清，当不确定性笼罩一切时，我们最容易将他人的行为视为正确之举。

In the process of examining the reactions of other people to resolve our uncertainty, however, we are likely to overlook a subtle but important fact. Those people are probably examining the social evidence, too. Especially in an ambiguous situation, the tendency for everyone to be looking to see what everyone else is doing can lead to a fascinating phenomenon called "pluralistic ignorance." A thorough understanding of the pluralistic ignorance phenomenon helps immeasurably to explain a regular occurrence in our country that has been termed both a riddle and a national disgrace: the failure of entire groups of bystanders to aid victims in agonizing need of help.

然而，在试图通过观察他人的反应来消除疑虑的过程中，我们很可能会忽略一个微妙却重要的事实：其他人可能也在观察社会舆论。尤其是在情况不明朗的情况下，每个人都倾向于观察其他人的行动，这会导致一种被称为“多元无知”的奇特现象。深入理解多元无知现象，对于解释我国一个屡见不鲜、既令人费解又令人蒙羞的现象至关重要：当受害者痛苦不堪、急需帮助时，旁观者群体却袖手旁观，任由受害者遭受伤害。

The classic example of such bystander inaction and the one that has produced the most debate in journalistic, political, and scientific circles began as an ordinary homicide case in the borough of Queens in New York City. A woman in her late twenties, Catherine Genovese, was killed in a late-night attack on her home street as she returned from work. Murder is never an act to be passed off lightly, but in a city the size and tenor of New York, the Genovese incident warranted no more space than a fraction of a column in The New York Times. Catherine Genovese's story would have died with her on that day in March 1964 if it hadn't been for a mistake.

旁观者袖手旁观的经典案例，也是在新闻界、政界和科学界引发最多争论的案例，起源于纽约市皇后区的一起普通凶杀案。二十多岁的凯瑟琳·吉诺维斯（Catherine Genovese）在深夜下班回家的路上，在她家门前的街道上遭到袭击身亡。谋杀绝非儿戏，但在纽约这样规模庞大、氛围浓厚的城市里，吉诺维斯案在《纽约时报》上却只占了寥寥几笔。如果不是一个错误，凯瑟琳·吉诺维斯的故事或许会随着她1964年3月的离世而彻底消失。

The metropolitan editor of the Times , A. M. Rosenthal, happened to be having lunch with the city police commissioner a week later. Rosenthal asked the commissioner about a different Queens-based homicide, and the commissioner, thinking he was being questioned about the Genovese case, revealed something staggering that had been uncovered by the police investigation. It was something that left everyone who heard it, the commissioner included, aghast and grasping for explanations. Catherine Genovese had not experienced a quick, muffled death. It had been a long, loud, tortured, public event. Her assailant had chased and attacked her in the street three times over a period of thirty-five minutes before his knife finally silenced her cries for help. Incredibly, thirty-eight of her neighbors watched the events of her death unfold from the safety of their apartment windows without so much as lifting a finger to call the police.

一周后，《纽约时报》都市版编辑A·M·罗森塔尔恰巧与纽约市警察局长共进午餐。罗森塔尔向局长询问另一起发生在皇后区的凶杀案，局长误以为罗森塔尔是在询问吉诺维斯案，于是透露了警方调查中发现的惊人内幕。这番话令所有听到的人，包括局长本人，都震惊不已，百思不得其解。凯瑟琳·吉诺维斯并非死于一场短暂而悄无声息的死亡，而是一场漫长、喧闹、痛苦且公开的惨剧。在长达35分钟的时间里，凶手在街上追赶并袭击了她三次，最终用刀夺去了她的生命，结束了她最后的呼救。令人难以置信的是，她的38位邻居竟然在自家公寓的窗户边目睹了这一切，却无人报警。

Rosenthal, a former Pulitzer Prize—winning reporter, knew a story when he heard one. On the day of his lunch with the commissioner, he assigned a reporter to investigate the "bystander angle" of the Genovese incident. Within a week, the Times published a long, page 1 article that was to create a swirl of controversy and speculation. The first few paragraphs of that report provide the tone and focus of the burgeoning story:

罗森塔尔曾是普利策奖得主，他一听就知道这是个新闻。在他与专员共进午餐的当天，他指派了一名记者调查吉诺维斯事件中的“旁观者视角”。不到一周，《纽约时报》就刊登了一篇长篇报道，占据了头版，引发了轩然大波，各种猜测也随之而来。这篇报道的开头几段就奠定了整个事件的基调和焦点：

For more than half an hour thirty-eight respectable, law-abiding citizens in Queens watched a killer stalk and stab a woman in three separate attacks in Kew Gardens.
在皇后区的邱园，38 位体面守法的市民目睹了一名杀手跟踪并三次刺伤一名女子长达半个多小时。
Twice the sound of their voices and the sudden glow of their bedroom lights interrupted him and frightened him off. Each time he returned, sought her out, and stabbed her again. Not one person telephoned the police during the assault; one witness called after the woman was dead.
两次，她们的说话声和卧室灯光突然亮起，打断了他的行动，吓跑了他。每次他都返回，找到她，再次刺伤她。袭击发生时，没有一个人报警；只有一名目击者在女子死后报了警。
That was two weeks ago today. But Assistant Chief Inspector Frederick M. Lussen, in charge of the borough's detectives and a veteran of twenty-five years of homicide investigations, is still shocked.
那是两周前的今天。但负责该区侦探工作的助理总督察弗雷德里克·M·卢森，一位拥有25年凶杀案调查经验的老手，仍然感到震惊。
He can give a matter-of-fact recitation of many murders. But the Kew Gardens slaying baffles him—not because it is a murder, but because "good people" failed to call the police.
他能如数家珍地列举出许多谋杀案。但邱园凶杀案却让他百思不得其解——并非因为它是一起谋杀案，而是因为“好心人”竟然没有报警。

As with Assistant Chief Inspector Lussen, shock and bafflement were the standard reactions of almost everyone who learned the story's details. The shock struck first, leaving the police, the news-people, and the reading public stunned. The bafflement followed quickly. How could thirty-eight "good people" fail to act under those circumstances? No one could understand it. Even the murder witnesses themselves were bewildered. "I don't know," they answered one after another. "I just don't know." A few offered weak reasons for their inaction. For example, two or three people explained that they were "afraid" or "did not want to get involved." But these reasons do not stand up to close scrutiny: A simple anonymous call to the police could have saved Catherine Genovese without threatening the witness's future safety or free time. No, it wasn't the observers' fear or reluctance to complicate their lives that explained their lack of action; something else was going on there that even they could not fathom.

与助理总督察卢森一样，震惊和困惑几乎是所有了解事件细节的人的共同反应。震惊首先袭来，令警方、新闻工作者和广大读者都目瞪口呆。困惑紧随其后。三十八位“好人”在那种情况下怎么会袖手旁观？没有人能够理解。就连谋杀案的目击者自己也感到困惑。“我不知道，”他们一个接一个地回答，“我真的不知道。”有些人给出了站不住脚的理由来解释他们的不作为。例如，两三个人解释说他们“害怕”或“不想卷入其中”。但这些理由经不起推敲：只需匿名报警，就能在不影响目击者未来安全或自由时间的情况下，救下凯瑟琳·吉诺维斯。不，并非是目击者的恐惧或不愿让自己的生活变得复杂才导致他们无所作为；背后肯定还有其他原因，连他们自己都无法理解。

Confusion, though, does not make for good news copy. So the press as well as the other media—several papers, TV stations, and magazines were pursuing follow-up stories by now—emphasized the only explanation available at the time: The witnesses, no different from the rest of us, hadn't cared enough to get involved. We were becoming a nation of selfish, insensitive people. The rigors of modern life, especially city life, were hardening us. We were becoming "The Cold Society," unfeeling and indifferent to the plight of our fellow citizens.

然而，混乱的局面不利于新闻报道。因此，包括报纸、电视台和杂志在内的媒体——此时已有数家报纸、电视台和杂志开始跟进报道——都强调了当时唯一可行的解释：目击者和我们其他人一样，漠不关心，不愿伸出援手。我们正在变成一个自私冷漠的民族。现代生活的艰辛，尤其是城市生活的艰辛，正在使我们变得冷酷无情。我们正在变成“冷漠社会”，对同胞的困境麻木不仁。

In support of this interpretation, news stories began appearing regularly in which various kinds of public apathy were detailed. The Times actually appears to have developed an apathy "beat" for a period following the Genovese revelations. Also supporting such an interpretation were the remarks of a range of armchair social commentators, who, as a breed, seem never to admit to bafflement when speaking to the press. They, too, saw the Genovese case as having large-scale social significance. All used the word "apathy," which, it is interesting to note, had been in the headline of the Times 's front-page story, although they accounted for the apathy differently. One attributed it to the effects of TV violence, another to repressed aggressiveness, but most implicated the "depersonalization" of urban life with its "megalopolitan societies" and its "alienation of the individual from the group." Even Rosenthal, the newsman who first broke the story and who ulti-mately made it the subject of a book, subscribed to the city-caused apathy theory.

为了佐证这种解读，新闻报道开始频繁出现，详细描述了各种形式的公众冷漠。事实上，《纽约时报》似乎在吉诺维斯案曝光后的一段时间内专门开辟了一条关于冷漠的“报道”路线。此外，一些纸上谈兵的社会评论员也支持这种解读，这类评论员似乎从不在媒体面前承认自己感到困惑。他们也认为吉诺维斯案具有广泛的社会意义。所有人都使用了“冷漠”一词，值得注意的是，《纽约时报》头版报道的标题也使用了这个词，尽管他们对这种冷漠的解释各不相同。有人将其归因于电视暴力的影响，有人归因于被压抑的攻击性，但大多数人认为这与都市生活的“去人格化”及其“大都市社会”以及“个体与群体的疏离”有关。就连最先报道此事并最终将其写成书的新闻记者罗森塔尔也认同城市造成冷漠的理论。

Nobody can say why the thirty-eight did not lift the phone while Miss Genovese was being attacked, since they cannot say themselves. It can be assumed, however, that their apathy was indeed one of the big-city variety. It is almost a matter of psychological survival, if one is surrounded and pressed by millions of people, to prevent them from constantly impinging on you, and the only way to do this is to ignore them as often as possible. Indifference to one's neighbor and his troubles is a conditioned reflex in life in New York as it is in other big cities.
没人能说清为什么那38个人在吉诺维斯小姐遇袭时没有拿起电话，因为他们自己也无法解释。不过，可以推测，他们的冷漠确实是大都市特有的。身处人潮汹涌的大都市，为了避免被他们不断打扰，几乎是一种心理上的生存本能，而唯一的办法就是尽可能地忽略他们。在纽约，如同在其他大城市一样，对邻居及其困境漠不关心是一种条件反射。

As the Genovese story grew—aside from Rosenthal's book, it became the focus of numerous newspaper and magazine pieces, several television-news documentaries, and an off-Broadway play—it attracted the professional attention of a pair of New York-based psychology professors, Bibb Latane and John Darley. They examined the reports of the Genovese incident and, on the basis of their knowledge of social psychology, hit on what had seemed the most unlikely explanation of all—it was that thirty-eight witnesses were present. Previous accounts of the story had invariably emphasized that no action was taken, even though thirty-eight individuals had looked on. Latane and Darley suggested that no one had helped precisely because there were so many observers. The psychologists speculated that, for at least two reasons, a bystander to an emergency would be unlikely to help when there were a number of other bystanders present. The first reason is fairly straightforward. With several potential helpers around, the personal responsibility of each individual is reduced: "Perhaps someone else will give or call for aid, perhaps someone else already has." So with everyone thinking that someone else will help or has helped, no one does.

随着吉诺维斯事件的传播——除了罗森塔尔的著作外，它还成为众多报纸杂志报道、几部电视新闻纪录片以及一部外百老汇戏剧的焦点——它引起了两位纽约心理学教授比布·拉坦和约翰·达利的专业关注。他们研究了吉诺维斯事件的报道，并基于他们的社会心理学知识，提出了一个看似最不可能的解释——当时有38名目击者在场。此前对该事件的报道无一例外地强调，尽管有38个人在场，但没有人采取任何行动。拉坦和达利认为，正是因为有这么多旁观者，才导致无人伸出援手。这两位心理学家推测，至少有两个原因会导致在紧急情况下，当有多名旁观者在场时，一个人不太可能伸出援手。第一个原因相当简单明了。周围有好几个潜在的帮手，每个人的责任感就降低了：“也许别人会伸出援手或者寻求帮助，也许别人已经这么做了。”所以，大家都觉得别人会帮忙或者已经帮忙了，结果反而没有人出手相助。

The second reason is the more psychologically intriguing one; it is founded on the principle of social proof and involves the pluralistic ignorance effect. Very often an emergency is not obviously an emergency. Is the man lying in the alley a heart-attack victim or a drunk sleeping one off? Are the sharp sounds from the street gunshots or truck backfires? Is the commotion next door an assault requiring the police or an especially loud marital spat where intervention would be inappropriate and unwelcome? What is going on? In times of such uncertainty, the natural tendency is to look around at the actions of others for clues.

第二个原因更具心理学趣味性；它基于社会认同原则，并涉及多元无知效应。很多时候，紧急情况并非显而易见。躺在巷子里的人是心脏病发作的受害者，还是醉酒后昏睡的醉汉？街上传来的尖锐声响是枪声还是卡车回火？隔壁的骚动是需要警察介入的袭击事件，还是音量特别大的夫妻争吵，不宜介入且不受欢迎？到底发生了什么？在这种不确定的情况下，人们自然会倾向于观察周围其他人的行为以寻找线索。

We can learn, from the way the other witnesses are reacting, whether the event is or is not an emergency.

我们可以从其他目击者的反应中得知，这起事件是否属于紧急情况。

What is easy to forget, though, is that everybody else observing the event is likely to be looking for social evidence, too. And because we all prefer to appear poised and unflustered among others, we are likely to search for that evidence placidly, with brief, camouflaged glances at those around us. Therefore everyone is likely to see everyone else looking unruffled and failing to act. As a result, and by the principle of social proof, the event will be roundly interpreted as a nonemergency. This, according to Latane and Darley, is the state of pluralistic ignorance "in which each person decides that since nobody is concerned, nothing is wrong. Meanwhile, the danger may be mounting to the point where a single individual, uninfluenced by the seeming calm of others, would react."

然而，人们很容易忘记的是，其他所有观察事件的人也可能都在寻找社会证据。由于我们都倾向于在他人面前表现得镇定自若，我们很可能会平静地寻找这种证据，只是偶尔瞥一眼周围的人，眼神中带着一丝不易察觉的意味。因此，每个人都可能看到其他人看起来都镇定自若，没有采取任何行动。结果，根据社会认同原则，该事件将被普遍解读为非紧急情况。拉坦和达利认为，这就是多元无知的状态，“在这种状态下，每个人都认为既然没有人感到担忧，那就说明一切正常。与此同时，危险可能正在加剧，以至于某个不受他人表面平静影响的人会采取行动。”

The fascinating upshot of Latane and Darley's reasoning is that, for the emergency victim, the idea of "safety in numbers" may often be completely wrong. It might be that someone in need of emergency aid would have a better chance of survival if a single bystander, rather than a crowd, was present. To test this unusual thesis, Darley, Latane, their students and colleagues performed a systematic and impressive program of research that produced a clear set of findings. Their basic procedure was to stage emergency events that were observed either by a single individual or by a group of people. They then recorded the number of times the emergency victim received help under those circumstances. In their first experiment, a New York college student who appeared to be having an epileptic seizure received help 85 percent of the time when there was a single bystander present but only 31 percent of the time with five bystanders present. With almost all the single bystanders helping, it becomes difficult to argue that ours is "The Cold Society" where no one cares for suffering others. Obviously it was something about the presence of other bystanders that reduced helping to shameful levels.

拉坦和达利的论证得出了一个引人入胜的结论：对于紧急情况下的受害者而言，“人多力量大”的观念可能常常完全错误。或许，如果现场只有一位旁观者，而不是一群人，那么需要紧急救助的人反而更有可能生存下来。为了验证这一不同寻常的论点，达利、拉坦及其学生和同事开展了一项系统而令人印象深刻的研究，并得出了一系列清晰的结论。他们的基本方法是模拟紧急情况，分别由一名旁观者或一群人观察。然后，他们记录了在这些情况下，受害者获得帮助的次数。在他们的第一个实验中，一位纽约大学生在癫痫发作时，如果只有一位旁观者在场，他获得帮助的概率为85%；而如果现场有五位旁观者，则只有31%的概率获得帮助。几乎所有旁观者都伸出援手，这使得我们很难再说我们生活在一个“冷漠社会”，没有人关心他人的痛苦。显然，正是其他旁观者的存在，才使得助人行为减少到令人羞耻的地步。

Other studies have examined the importance of social proof in causing widespread witness "apathy." They have done so by planting within a group of witnesses to a possible emergency people who are rehearsed to act as if no emergency were occurring. For instance, in another New York—based experiment, 75 percent of lone individuals who observed smoke seeping from under a door reported the leak; however, when similar leaks were observed by three-person groups, the smoke was reported only 38 percent of the time. The smallest number of bystanders took action, though, when the three-person groups included two individuals who had been coached to ignore the smoke; under those conditions, the leaks were reported only 10 percent of the time. In a similar study conducted in Toronto, single bystanders provided emergency aid 90 percent of the time, whereas such aid occurred in only 16 percent of the cases when a bystander was in the presence of two other bystanders who remained passive.

其他研究也探讨了社会认同在导致目击者普遍“冷漠”方面的重要性。他们通过在可能发生紧急情况的目击者群体中安排一些经过训练的人，让他们装作若无其事，以此来验证社会认同的作用。例如，在另一项于纽约进行的实验中，75%的单独目击者在观察到门缝下渗烟时会报告；然而，当三人小组观察到类似的渗漏时，只有38%的人会报告。但当三人小组中有两人被训练成对烟雾视而不见时，采取行动的旁观者人数最少；在这种情况下，只有10%的人会报告渗漏。在多伦多进行的一项类似研究中，90%的单独目击者会提供紧急援助，而当一名目击者身边有两名保持沉默的旁观者时，只有16%的人会提供援助。

After more than a decade of such research, social scientists now have a good idea of when a bystander will offer emergency aid. First, and contrary to the view that we have become a society of callous, uncaring people, once witnesses are convinced that an emergency situation exists, aid is very likely. Under these conditions, the numbers of bystanders who either intervene themselves or summon help is quite comforting. For example, in four separate experiments done in Florida, accident scenes involving a maintenance man were staged. When it was clear that the man was hurt and required assistance, he was helped 100 percent of the time in two of the experiments. In the other two experiments, where helping involved contact with potentially dangerous electrical wires, the victim still received bystander aid in 90 percent of the instances. In addition, these extremely high levels of assistance occurred whether the witnesses observed the event singly or in groups. 9

经过十多年的研究，社会科学家现在对旁观者何时会提供紧急援助有了较为清晰的认识。首先，与人们普遍认为我们已经变成了一个冷漠无情的社会的观点相反，一旦目击者确信存在紧急情况，他们很可能会伸出援手。在这种情况下，那些主动介入或寻求帮助的旁观者人数之多令人欣慰。例如，在佛罗里达州进行的四项独立实验中，研究人员模拟了涉及一名维修工的事故现场。当该男子明显受伤需要帮助时，其中两项实验中，他100%都得到了帮助。在另外两项实验中，即使帮助涉及接触可能危险的电线，受害者仍然在90%的情况下得到了旁观者的帮助。此外，无论目击者是单独观察还是结伴而行，都出现了如此高的援助率。

The situation becomes very different when, as in many cases, bystanders cannot be sure that the event they are witnessing is an emergency. Then a victim is much more likely to be helped by a lone bystander than by a group, especially if the people in the group are strangers to one another. It seems that the pluralistic ignorance effect is strongest among strangers: Because we like to look poised and sophisticated in public and because we are unfamiliar with the reactions of those we do not know, we are unlikely to give off or correctly read expressions of concern when in a grouping of strangers. Therefore, a possible emergency becomes viewed as a nonemergency, and the victim suffers.

当旁观者无法确定他们目睹的事件是否属于紧急情况时，情况就截然不同了，这种情况在很多情况下都会发生。此时，受害者更有可能得到单个旁观者的帮助，而不是一群人，尤其是在这群人彼此并不认识的情况下。似乎“多元无知效应”在陌生人之间最为显著：因为我们喜欢在公共场合保持镇定和老练，而且我们不熟悉陌生人的反应，所以在陌生人群体中，我们不太可能表现出或正确解读他人的关心。因此，潜在的紧急情况会被误认为是非紧急情况，受害者因此遭受痛苦。

A close look at this set of research findings reveals an enlightening pattern. All the conditions that decrease an emergency victim's chances for bystander aid exist normally and innocently in the city: (1) In contrast to rural areas, cities are more clamorous, distracting, rapidly changing places where it is difficult to be certain of the nature of the events one encounters. (2) Urban environments are more populous, by their nature; consequently, people are more likely to be with others when witnessing a potential emergency situation. (3) City dwellers know a much smaller percentage of fellow residents than do people who live in small towns; therefore, city dwellers are more likely to find themselves in a group of strangers when observing an emergency.

仔细分析这组研究结果，可以发现一个发人深省的模式。所有会降低紧急情况下受害者获得旁观者帮助机会的因素，在城市中都普遍存在，而且往往不易察觉：（1）与乡村地区相比，城市更加喧闹、令人分心、变化迅速，人们很难确定所遇事件的性质。（2）城市环境本身人口密度就更高；因此，人们在目睹潜在的紧急情况时更有可能与他人在一起。（3）城市居民认识的邻居比例远低于小城镇居民；因此，城市居民在目睹紧急情况时更有可能身处一群陌生人之中。

These three natural characteristics of urban environments—their confusion, their populousness, and their low levels of acquaintanceship—fit in very well with the factors shown by research to decrease bystander aid. Without ever having to resort to such sinister concepts as "urban depersonalization" and "megalopolitan alienation," then, we can explain why so many instances of bystander inaction occur in our cities.

城市环境的这三个自然特征——混乱、人口密集和人与人之间熟识度低——与研究表明导致旁观者不施以援手的因素非常吻合。因此，我们无需诉诸“城市去人性化”和“大都市疏离”等耸人听闻的概念，就能解释为何城市中会出现如此多的旁观者不作为事件。

# ↩

Devictimizing Yourself

伤害自己

But explaining the dangers of modern urban life in less ominous terms does not dispel them. And as the world's populations move increasingly to the cities—half of all humanity will be city dwellers within ten years—there will be a growing need to reduce those dangers. Fortunately, our newfound understanding of the bystander "apathy" process offers real hope. Armed with this scientific knowledge, an emergency victim can increase enormously the chances of receiving aid from others. The key is the realization that groups of bystanders fail to help because the bystanders are unsure rather than unkind. They don't help because they are unsure of whether an emergency actually exists and whether they are responsible for taking action. When they are sure of their responsibilities for intervening in a clear emergency, people are exceedingly responsive!

但用不那么耸人听闻的措辞来解释现代都市生活的危险并不能消除这些危险。随着世界人口不断向城市迁移——十年内，全球一半人口将成为城市居民——减少这些危险的需求将日益增长。幸运的是，我们对旁观者“冷漠”过程的新认识带来了真正的希望。掌握了这些科学知识，紧急情况下的受害者就能大大增加获得他人帮助的机会。关键在于认识到，旁观者群体之所以不伸出援手，是因为他们犹豫不决，而非心怀恶意。他们不提供帮助，是因为他们不确定紧急情况是否真的存在，以及自己是否有责任采取行动。当他们确信自己有责任在明确的紧急情况下进行干预时，人们的反应会异常积极！

Once it is understood that the enemy is not some unmanageable societal condition like urban depersonalization but is, instead, the simple state of uncertainty, it becomes possible for emergency victims to take specific steps to protect themselves by reducing the bystanders' uncertainty. Imagine, for example, you are spending a summer afternoon at a music concert in the park. As the concert ends and people begin leaving, you notice a slight numbness in one arm but dismiss it as nothing to be alarmed about. Yet, while moving with the crowd to the distant parking areas, you feel the numbness spreading down to your hand and up one side of your face. Feeling disoriented, you decide to sit against a tree for a moment to rest. Soon you realize that something is drastically wrong. Sitting down has not helped; in fact, the control and coordination of your muscles has worsened to the point that you are starting to have difficulty moving your mouth and tongue to speak. You try to get up but can't. A terrifying thought slashes to mind: "Oh, God, I'm having a stroke!" Groups of people are passing by and most are paying you no attention. The few who notice the odd way you are slumped against the tree or the strange look on your face check the social evidence around them and, seeing that no one else is reacting with concern, walk on past convinced that nothing is wrong.

一旦人们意识到敌人并非像城市人格解体那样难以控制的社会问题，而是单纯的不确定状态，那么紧急情况下的受害者就可以通过降低旁观者的不确定性来采取具体措施保护自己。例如，想象一下，你在一个夏日的午后在公园里听音乐会。音乐会结束，人们开始离开时，你注意到一只手臂有些麻木，但你觉得没什么大不了的。然而，当你随着人群走向远处的停车场时，你感到麻木感蔓延到你的手，并向上延伸到半边脸。你感到一阵眩晕，于是决定靠着一棵树坐一会儿休息。很快，你意识到情况非常不妙。坐下并没有缓解你的不适；事实上，你的肌肉控制和协调能力恶化到你开始难以控制嘴巴和舌头说话的地步。你试图站起来，却动弹不得。一个可怕的念头闪过脑海：“天哪，我中风了！”一群群人从你身边经过，大多数人都没有注意到你。少数注意到你倚靠在树上的奇怪姿势或你脸上异样表情的人，会环顾四周，看看周围的人是否都表示关心，然后便径直走开，认为一切正常。

Were you to find yourself in such a predicament, what could you do to overcome the odds against receiving help? Because your physical abilities would be deteriorating, time would be crucial. If, before you could summon aid, you lost your speech or mobility or consciousness, your chances for assistance and for recovery would plunge drastically. It would be essential to try to request help quickly. But what would the most effective form of that request be? Moans, groans, or outcries probably would not do. They might bring you some attention, but they would not provide enough information to assure passersby that a true emergency existed.

如果你不幸身处这种困境，该如何克服求助的难关？由于你的身体机能会不断下降，时间至关重要。如果你在求助前失去了说话能力、行动能力或意识，那么你获得帮助和康复的几率将骤然降低。因此，迅速寻求帮助至关重要。但最有效的求助方式是什么呢？呻吟、哀嚎或呼救可能都无济于事。它们或许能引起一些人的注意，但却无法提供足够的信息让路人确信你正处于真正的紧急情况。

If mere outcries are unlikely to produce help from the passing crowd, perhaps you should be more specific. Indeed, you need to do more than try to gain attention; you should call out clearly your need for assistance. You must not allow bystanders to define your situation as a nonemergency. Use the word "Help" to cry out your need for emergency aid. And don't worry about being wrong. Embarrassment is a villain to be crushed here. In the context of a possible stroke, you cannot afford to be worried about the awkwardness of overestimating your problem. The difference in cost is that between a moment of embarrassment and possible death or lifelong paralysis.

如果仅仅呼救不太可能引起路人的注意，或许你应该更具体地说明你的需求。事实上，你需要做的不仅仅是吸引注意力；你应该清晰地表达你的求助。你绝不能让旁观者将你的情况定义为非紧急情况。用“救命”这个词来呼救，表明你需要紧急救助。不要担心自己说错了。此时此刻，尴尬是必须克服的障碍。在可能发生中风的情况下，你根本无法承受高估自身问题的尴尬。这其中的代价是：一时的尴尬和可能的死亡或终身瘫痪之间的差别。

But even a resounding call for help is not your most effective tactic. Although it may reduce bystanders' doubts about whether a real emergency exists, it will not remove several other important uncertainties within each onlooker's mind: What kind of aid is required here? Should I be the one to provide the aid, or should someone more qualified do it? Has someone else already gone to get professional help, or is it my responsibility? While the bystanders stand gawking at you and grappling with these questions, time vital to your survival could be slipping away.

但即便大声呼救，也并非最有效的策略。虽然这或许能消除旁观者对紧急情况是否真的存在的疑虑，但却无法消除他们心中其他几个重要的疑问：这里需要什么样的帮助？我应该亲自施救，还是应该由更专业的人员来做？是否有人已经寻求专业帮助，还是我应该主动出击？当旁观者们围观你、纠结于这些问题时，关乎你生存的宝贵时间可能正在悄然流逝。

Clearly, then, as a victim you must do more than alert bystanders to your need for emergency assistance; you must also remove their uncertainties about how that assistance should be provided and who should provide it. But what would be the most efficient and reliable way to do so?

显然，作为受害者，你不仅要提醒旁观者你需要紧急援助，还要消除他们对如何提供援助以及由谁提供援助的疑虑。但最有效、最可靠的方法是什么呢？

Based on the research findings we have seen, my advice would be to isolate one individual from the crowd: Stare, speak, and point directly at that person and no one else: "You, sir, in the blue jacket, I need help. Call an ambulance." With that one utterance you should dispel all the uncertainties that might prevent or delay help. With that one statement you will have put the man in the blue jacket in the role of "rescuer." He should now understand that emergency aid is needed; he should understand that he, not someone else, is responsible for providing the aid; and, finally, he should understand exactly how to provide it. All the scientific evidence indicates that the result should be quick, effective assistance.

根据我们掌握的研究结果，我的建议是：从人群中单独挑选一个人，盯着他看，指着他，只指着他：“先生，穿蓝色夹克的那位，我需要帮助。请叫救护车。” 这句话就能消除所有可能阻碍或延误救援的疑虑。这句话就能让穿蓝色夹克的那位男士扮演“救援者”的角色。他现在应该明白需要紧急救助；他应该明白，提供救助的责任在他自己身上，而不是其他人；最后，他应该清楚地知道如何提供救助。所有科学证据都表明，这样做能够迅速有效地提供帮助。

In general, then, your best strategy when in need of emergency help is to reduce the uncertainties of those around you concerning your condition and their responsibilities. Be as precise as possible about your need for aid. Do not allow bystanders to come to their own conclusions because, especially in a crowd, the principle of social proof and the consequent pluralistic ignorance effect might well cause them to view your situation as a nonemergency.

因此，一般来说，当你需要紧急帮助时，最好的策略是尽量减少周围人对你的情况以及他们应承担的责任的不确定性。尽可能准确地说明你需要帮助的原因。不要让旁观者自行判断，因为尤其是在人群中，社会认同原则以及由此产生的多元无知效应很可能导致他们将你的情况视为非紧急情况。

And request assistance of a single individual from the group of onlookers. Fight the natural tendency to make a general request for help. Pick out one person and assign the task to that individual. Otherwise, it is too easy for everyone in the crowd to assume that someone else should help, will help, or has helped. Of all the techniques in this book designed to produce compliance with a request, this one may be the most important to remember. After all, the failure of your request for emergency aid could have severe personal consequences.

然后向围观人群中的一位求助者寻求帮助。克服想要泛泛求助的本能。选定一个人，并将任务分配给他/她。否则，人群很容易想当然地认为其他人应该、将会或已经伸出援手。本书中所有旨在促使他人配合的技巧中，这或许是最重要的一条。毕竟，你的紧急求助若被拒绝，可能会给你带来严重的个人后果。

Not long ago, I received some firsthand evidence on this point. I was involved in a rather serious automobile collision. Both I and the other driver were plainly hurt: He was slumped, unconscious, over his steering wheel while I managed to stagger, bloody, from behind mine. The accident had occurred in the center of an intersection in full view of several individuals stopped in their cars at the traffic light. As I knelt in the road beside my door, trying to clear my head, the light changed and the waiting cars began to roll slowly through the intersection; their drivers gawked but did not stop.

不久前，我亲身经历了这件事。我卷入了一场相当严重的车祸。我和另一位司机都受了重伤：他瘫倒在方向盘上，昏迷不醒；而我浑身是血，踉跄着从车后站了起来。事故发生在十字路口中央，当时有好几辆车停在红绿灯前，目睹了整个过程。我跪在车门旁的路上，试图让自己清醒过来，这时绿灯变绿了，那些停着的车开始缓缓驶过路口；司机们都愣住了，但没有停车。

I remember thinking, "Oh no, it's happening just like the research says. They're all passing by!" I consider it fortunate that, as a social psychologist, I knew enough about the bystander studies to have that particular thought. By thinking of my predicament in terms of the research findings, I knew exactly what to do. Pulling myself up so I could be seen clearly, I pointed at the driver of one car: "Call the police." To a second and a third driver, pointing directly each time: "Pull over, we need help." The responses of these people were instantaneous. They summoned a police car and ambulance immediately, they used their handkerchiefs to blot the blood from my face, they put a jacket under my head, they volunteered to serve as witnesses to the accident; one even offered to ride with me to the hospital.

我记得当时心想：“糟了，这跟研究里说的完全一样。他们都视而不见！” 我很庆幸自己作为一名社会心理学家，对旁观者效应研究有所了解，所以才想到这一点。通过运用研究成果来分析我的困境，我立刻知道该怎么做。我站起身，让自己能被清楚地看到，指着一辆车的司机说：“报警。” 我又指着第二辆和第三辆车的司机说：“靠边停车，我们需要帮助。” 这些人的反应非常迅速。他们立即叫来了警车和救护车，用手帕帮我擦掉脸上的血，把外套垫在我的头下，主动提出做事故目击证人；甚至有人提出要送我去医院。

Not only was this help rapid and solicitous, it was infectious. After drivers entering the intersection from the other direction saw cars stopping for me, they stopped and began tending to the other victim. The principle of social proof was working for us now. The trick had been to get the ball rolling in the direction of aid. Once that was accomplished, I was able to relax and let the bystanders' genuine concern and social proof's natural momentum do the rest.

这种帮助不仅迅速而贴心，而且还具有感染力。当对面方向驶入路口的司机看到有车停下来帮助我时，他们也停了下来，开始救助另一位伤者。社会认同的原理此刻对我们奏效了。关键在于如何让大家开始伸出援手。一旦做到这一点，我就可以放松下来，让旁观者真诚的关心和社会认同的自然作用力来完成剩下的工作。

MONKEY ME, MONKEY DO

猴子我，猴子做

A bit earlier we stated that the principle of social proof, like all other weapons of influence, works better under some conditions than under others. We have already explored one of those conditions: uncertainty. Without question, when people are uncertain, they are more likely to use others' actions to decide how they themselves should act. But, in addition, there is another important working condition: similarity. The principle of social proof operates most powerfully when we are observing the behavior of people just like us. It is the conduct of such people that gives us the greatest insight into what constitutes correct behavior for ourselves. Therefore we are more inclined to follow the lead of a similar individual than a dissimilar one.

我们之前提到过，社会认同原则和其他所有影响力手段一样，在某些条件下比其他条件下更有效。我们已经探讨过其中一个条件：不确定性。毫无疑问，当人们感到不确定时，他们更倾向于参考他人的行为来决定自己的行为。但除此之外，还有一个重要的条件：相似性。当我们观察与我们相似的人的行为时，社会认同原则的作用最为显著。正是这些人的行为让我们更深刻地认识到什么才是对自己而言正确的行为。因此，我们更倾向于效仿与自己相似的人，而不是与自己不同的人。

That is why I believe we are seeing an increasing number of average-person-on-the-street testimonials on TV these days. Advertisers now know that one successful way to sell a product to ordinary viewers (who compose the largest potential market) is to demonstrate that other "ordinary" people like and use it. So whether the product is a brand of soft drink, or a pain reliever, or a laundry detergent, we hear volleys of praise from John or Mary Every-person.

这就是为什么我认为如今电视上出现越来越多普通民众的证言的原因。广告商现在明白，向普通观众（他们构成了最大的潜在市场）推销产品的一个有效方法，就是展示其他“普通人”喜欢并使用该产品。因此，无论产品是某种软饮料、止痛药还是洗衣液，我们都能听到来自约翰或玛丽等普通人的赞誉之声。

More compelling evidence for the importance of similarity in determining whether we will imitate another's behavior comes from scientific research. An especially apt illustration can be found in a study done several years ago by Columbia University psychologists. The researchers placed wallets on the ground in various locations around midtown Manhattan to observe what would happen when they were found. The wallets all contained $2.00 in cash, a $26.30 check, and various information providing the name and address of the wallet's "owner." In addition to this material, the wallet also contained a letter that made it evident that the wallet had been lost not once, but twice. The letter was written to the wallet's owner from a man who had found it earlier and whose intention was to return it. The finder indicated in his letter that he was happy to help and that the chance to be of service in this way had made him feel good.

科学研究提供了更有力的证据，证明相似性在决定我们是否会模仿他人行为方面的重要性。哥伦比亚大学心理学家几年前进行的一项研究就是一个很好的例证。研究人员在曼哈顿中城的不同地点放置了一些钱包，观察人们发现钱包后的反应。每个钱包里都装有2美元现金、一张26.30美元的支票，以及一些信息，包括钱包“主人”的姓名和地址。除了这些物品外，钱包里还有一封信，信中表明钱包不止一次丢失，而是两次。这封信是一位之前捡到钱包的人写给钱包主人的，他打算归还钱包。捡到钱包的人在信中表示，他很乐意帮忙，能够以这种方式帮助别人让他感到很开心。

It was evident to anyone who found one of these wallets that this well-intentioned individual had then lost the wallet himself on the way to the mailbox—the wallet was wrapped in an envelope addressed to the owner. The researchers wanted to know how many people finding such a wallet would follow the lead of the first finder and mail it, intact, to the original owner. Before they dropped the wallets, however, the researchers varied one feature of the letter it contained. Some of the letters were written in standard English by what seemed to be an average American, while the other letters were written in broken English by the first finder, who identified himself as a recently arrived foreigner. In other words, the person who had initially found the wallet and had tried to return it was depicted by the letter as being either similar or dissimilar to most Americans.

任何捡到这些钱包的人都会发现，这位好心人是在去邮箱的路上弄丢了钱包——钱包被装在一个写着失主名字的信封里。研究人员想知道，有多少捡到钱包的人会效仿第一个捡到者，将钱包完好无损地寄回给失主。然而，在投放钱包之前，研究人员对信封里的信件做了一些改动。有些信件是用标准的英语写的，作者看起来像是一位普通的美国人；而另一些信件则是第一个捡到钱包的人用蹩脚的英语写的，他自称是一位刚到美国的外国人。换句话说，信件中对最初捡到钱包并试图归还的人的描述，要么与大多数美国人相似，要么与大多数美国人截然不同。

The interesting question was whether the Manhattanites who found the wallet and letter would be more influenced to mail the wallet if the first man who had tried to do so was similar to them. The answer was plain: Only 33 percent of the wallets were returned when the first finder was seen as dissimilar, but fully 70 percent were returned when he was thought to be a similar other. These results suggest an important qualification of the principle of social proof. We will use the actions of others to decide on proper behavior for ourselves, especially when we view those others as similar to ourselves.

一个有趣的问题是：如果第一个试图寄回钱包和信件的人与曼哈顿居民相似，那么这些居民是否会更倾向于寄回钱包？答案显而易见：当第一个拾获者被认为与他们不同时，只有33%的钱包被归还；而当拾获者被认为与他们相似时，归还率高达70%。这些结果表明，社会认同原则需要进行重要的修正。我们会参考他人的行为来决定自己的行为是否恰当，尤其当我们认为他人与自己相似时。

This tendency applies not only to adults but to children as well. Health researchers have found, for example, that a school-based antismoking program had lasting effects only when it used same-age peer leaders as teachers. Another study found that children who saw a film depicting a child's positive visit to the dentist lowered their own dental anxieties principally when they were the same age as the child in the film. I wish I had known about this second study when, a few years before it was published, I was trying to reduce a different kind of anxiety in my son, Chris.

这种趋势不仅适用于成人，也适用于儿童。例如，健康研究人员发现，只有当学校的戒烟项目由同龄同伴担任教师时，才能产生持久的效果。另一项研究发现，观看过描绘儿童愉快看牙医经历的影片的儿童，尤其是与影片中儿童年龄相仿的儿童，他们的牙科焦虑感会显著降低。几年前，当我试图帮助儿子克里斯缓解另一种焦虑时，我真希望自己当时就知道这项研究。

I live in Arizona, where backyard swimming pools abound. One regrettable consequence is that every year several young children drown after falling into an unattended pool. I was determined, therefore, to teach Chris how to swim at an early age. The problem was not that he was afraid of the water. He loved it. But he would not get into the pool without wearing his inflatable plastic inner tube, no matter how I tried to coax, talk, or shame him out of it. After getting nowhere for two months, I hired some help: a graduate student of mine—a big, strapping former lifeguard who had once worked as a swimming instructor. He failed as totally as I had. He couldn't persuade Chris to attempt even a stroke outside of his plastic ring.

我住在亚利桑那州，这里到处都是后院游泳池。令人遗憾的是，每年都有好几个小孩因为掉进无人看管的游泳池而溺水身亡。因此，我下定决心要从小就教克里斯游泳。问题不在于他怕水，他很喜欢水。但不管我怎么哄、怎么劝、怎么让他觉得不好意思，他都非得戴着充气塑料内胎才肯下水。两个月过去了，毫无进展，我只好请了个帮手：我的一个研究生——一个身材魁梧、体格健壮的前救生员，也当过游泳教练。结果他跟我一样彻底失败了。他根本没办法让克里斯脱下塑料圈，哪怕只是尝试一下划水。

Around this time, Chris was attending a day camp that provided a number of activities to its members, including use of a large pool, which he scrupulously avoided. One day, shortly after the graduate student fiasco, I went to get Chris from camp a bit early and, with mouth agape, watched him run down the diving board and jump into the middle of the deepest part of the pool. Panicking, I began pulling off my shoes to jump in to his rescue when I saw him bob to the surface and paddle safely to the side of the pool—where I dashed, shoes in hand, to meet him.

大约就在那时，克里斯参加了一个夏令营，营地提供各种活动，包括一个大型游泳池，但他总是刻意避开它。一天，就在研究生事件发生后不久，我提前去营地接克里斯，目瞪口呆地看着他跑下跳板，跳进了泳池最深的地方。我惊慌失措，正要脱鞋跳下去救他，却看到他浮出水面，安全地游到泳池边——我赶紧拿着鞋子冲过去接他。

"Chris, you can swim," I said excitedly. "You can swim!"

“克里斯，你会游泳！”我兴奋地说。“你会游泳！”

"Yes," he responded casually, "I learned how today."

“是的，”他漫不经心地回答，“我今天才学会的。”

"This is terrific! This is just terrific," I burbled, gesturing expansively to convey my enthusiasm. "But how come you didn't need your plastic ring today?"

“太棒了！真是太棒了！”我兴奋地说道，一边夸张地比划着手势。“可是，你今天怎么不需要你的塑料戒指呢？”

Looking somewhat embarrassed because his father seemed to be raving while inexplicably soaking his socks in a small puddle and waving his shoes around, Chris explained: "Well, I'm three years old, and Tommy is three years old. And Tommy can swim without a ring, so that means I can too."

克里斯看起来有些尴尬，因为他父亲似乎在胡言乱语，同时又莫名其妙地把袜子浸在一个小水坑里，还挥舞着鞋子。克里斯解释说：“嗯，我三岁，汤米也三岁。汤米不用游泳圈就能游泳，所以我也一样可以。”

I could have kicked myself. Of course, it would be to little Tommy, not to a six-foot-two-inch graduate student, that Chris would look for the most relevant information about what he could or should do. Had I been more thoughtful about solving Chris's swimming problem, I could have employed Tommy's good example earlier and, perhaps, have saved myself a couple of frustrating months. I could have simply noted at the day camp that Tommy was a swimmer and then arranged with his parents for the boys to spend a weekend afternoon swimming in our pool. My guess is that Chris's plastic ring would have been abandoned by the end of the day.

我真想狠狠地抽自己一巴掌。当然，克里斯应该向小汤米寻求关于他能做什么或应该做什么的最相关信息，而不是向一个身高六英尺二英寸的研究生寻求。如果我当初能更周全地考虑解决克里斯的游泳问题，我本可以更早地借鉴汤米的例子，或许就能省去几个月的烦恼。我本可以在夏令营的时候就注意到汤米会游泳，然后安排他的父母让孩子们周末下午来我们家的泳池游泳。我猜，到那天结束的时候，克里斯的塑料游泳圈肯定早就被他扔掉了。

Any factor that can spur 70 percent of New Yorkers to return a wallet (or can reduce the likelihood that kids will take up smoking or will fear a dentist visit) must be considered impressive. Yet research findings of this sort offer just a hint of the immense impact that the conduct of similar others has on human behavior. Other, more powerful examples exist. To my mind, the most telling illustration of this impact starts with a seemingly nonsensical statistic: After a suicide has made front-page news, airplanes—private planes, corporate jets, airliners—begin falling out of the sky at an alarming rate.

任何能促使70%的纽约人归还钱包（或降低儿童吸烟或害怕看牙医的可能性）的因素都足以令人印象深刻。然而，这类研究结果仅仅揭示了类似行为对人类行为的巨大影响的冰山一角。还有其他更有力的例子。在我看来，最能说明这种影响的例子始于一个看似荒谬的统计数据：每当一起自杀事件登上头版头条，飞机——无论是私人飞机、公务机还是客机——的坠毁率就会以惊人的速度上升。

For example, it has been shown that immediately following certain kinds of highly publicized suicide stories, the number of people who die in commercial-airline crashes increases by 1,000 percent! Even more alarming: The increase is not limited to airplane deaths. The number of automobile fatalities shoots up as well. What could possibly be responsible?

例如，有研究表明，在某些类型的自杀事件被大肆报道之后，商业航班空难的死亡人数会立即增加1000%！更令人震惊的是：这种增长不仅限于飞机事故，汽车事故的死亡人数也会激增。这究竟是什么原因造成的呢？

One explanation suggests itself immediately: The same social conditions that cause some people to commit suicide cause others to die accidentally. For instance, certain individuals, the suicide-prone, may react to stressful societal events (economic downturns, rising crime rates, international tensions) by ending it all. But others will react differently to these same events; they might become angry or impatient or nervous or distracted. To the degree that such people operate (or service) the cars and planes of our society, the vehicles will be less safe, and, consequently, we will see a sharp increase in the number of automobile and air fatalities.

一种解释显而易见：导致某些人自杀的社会环境，也会导致另一些人意外死亡。例如，某些有自杀倾向的人，可能会以结束生命的方式来应对压力巨大的社会事件（经济衰退、犯罪率上升、国际局势紧张）。但其他人对同样的事件则会有不同的反应；他们可能会变得愤怒、不耐烦、紧张或心不在焉。如果这类人更多地参与驾驶（或维修）我们社会的汽车和飞机，那么这些交通工具的安全性就会降低，因此，我们将会看到汽车和航空事故死亡人数急剧上升。

According to this "social conditions" interpretation, then, some of the same societal factors that cause intentional deaths also cause accidental ones, and that is why we find so strong a connection between suicide stories and fatal crashes. But another fascinating statistic indicates that this is not the correct explanation: Fatal crashes increase dramatically only in those regions where the suicide has been highly publicized. Other places, existing under similar social conditions, whose newspapers have not publicized the story, have shown no comparable jump in such fatalities. Furthermore, within those areas where newspaper space has been allotted, the wider the publicity given the suicide, the greater has been the rise in subsequent crashes. Thus it is not some set of common societal events that stimulates suicides on the one hand, and fatal accidents on the other. Instead it is the publicized suicide story itself that produces the car and plane wrecks.

根据这种“社会条件”的解释，导致故意死亡的某些社会因素也会导致意外死亡，这就是为什么我们发现自杀事件与致命车祸之间存在如此紧密的联系。但另一项引人注目的统计数据表明，这并非正确的解释：致命车祸的急剧增加仅发生在自杀事件被广泛报道的地区。其他社会条件相似但报纸没有报道自杀事件的地区，此类死亡人数并未出现类似的激增。此外，在那些报纸版面被报道的地区，自杀事件的报道范围越广，后续车祸的增幅就越大。因此，并非某些常见的社会事件一方面刺激了自杀，另一方面又刺激了致命事故。相反，正是被广泛报道的自杀事件本身导致了车祸和空难的发生。

To explain the strong association between suicide-story publicity and subsequent crashes, a "bereavement" account has been suggested. Because, it has been argued, front-page suicides often in-volve well-known and respected public figures, perhaps their highly publicized deaths throw many people into states of shocked sadness. Stunned and preoccupied, these individuals become careless around cars and planes. The consequence is the sharp increase in deadly accidents involving such vehicles that we see after front-page suicide stories. Although the bereavement theory can account for the connection between the degree of publicity given a story and subsequent crash fatalities—the more people who learn of the suicide, the larger number of bereaved and careless individuals there will be—it cannot explain yet another startling fact: Newspaper stories reporting on suicide victims who died alone produce an increase in the frequency of single-fatality wrecks only, whereas stories reporting on suicide-plus-murder incidents produce an increase in multiple-fatality wrecks only. Simple bereavement could not cause such a pattern.

为了解释自杀新闻报道与后续交通事故之间的密切关联，有人提出了“丧亲之痛”理论。该理论认为，头版头条的自杀事件往往涉及知名且受人尊敬的公众人物，或许他们备受瞩目的死亡事件会令许多人陷入震惊和悲痛之中。这些人在震惊和忧虑中变得粗心大意，尤其是在驾驶汽车和飞机时。其结果就是，在头版自杀新闻报道之后，涉及此类交通工具的致命事故数量急剧增加。虽然丧亲之痛理论可以解释新闻报道程度与后续交通事故死亡人数之间的联系——知道自杀事件的人越多，悲痛和粗心大意的人就越多——但它却无法解释另一个令人震惊的事实：报道独自自杀者的新闻只会导致单人死亡事故的增加，而报道自杀加谋杀事件的新闻只会导致多人死亡事故的增加。单纯的丧亲之痛无法造成这种模式。

The influence of suicide stories on car and plane crashes, then, is fantastically specific. Stories of pure suicides, in which only one person dies, generate wrecks in which only one person dies; stories of suicide-murder combinations, in which there are multiple deaths, generate wrecks in which there are multiple deaths. If neither "social conditions" nor "bereavement" account for this bewildering array of facts, what can? There is a sociologist at the University of California at San Diego who thinks he has found the answer. His name is David Phillips, and he points a convincing finger at something called the "Werther effect."

因此，自杀故事对车祸和空难的影响具有惊人的特殊性。纯粹的自杀故事（即只有一人死亡）会导致只有一人死亡的事故；自杀与谋杀相结合的故事（即有多人死亡）会导致有多人死亡的事故。如果“社会条件”和“丧亲之痛”都无法解释这一系列令人费解的现象，那么究竟是什么原因呢？加州大学圣地亚哥分校的一位社会学家认为他找到了答案。他名叫大卫·菲利普斯，他令人信服地指出，这要归咎于一种叫做“维特效应”的现象。

The story of the Werther effect is both chilling and intriguing. More than two centuries ago, the great man of German literature, Johann von Goethe, published a novel entitled Die Leiden des jungen Werthers (The Sorrows of Young Werther). The book, in which the hero, named Werther, commits suicide, had a remarkable impact. Not only did it provide Goethe with immediate fame, but it also sparked a wave of emulative suicides across Europe. So powerful was this effect that authorities in several countries banned the novel.

“维特效应”的故事既令人不寒而栗，又引人入胜。两个多世纪前，德国文学巨匠约翰·冯·歌德出版了小说《少年维特的烦恼》（Die Leiden des jungen Werthers）。小说的主人公维特最终自杀，这部作品产生了巨大的影响。它不仅使歌德一举成名，还引发了席卷欧洲的效仿自杀浪潮。这种影响如此之大，以至于一些国家的当局甚至禁售了这部小说。

Professor Phillips's own work has traced the Werther effect to modern times. His research has demonstrated that immediately following a front-page suicide story the suicide rate increases dra-matically in those geographical areas where the story has been highly publicized. It is Phillips's argument that certain troubled people who read of another's self-inflicted death kill themselves in imitation. In a morbid illustration of the principle of social proof, these people decide how they should act on the basis of how some other troubled person has acted.

菲利普斯教授的研究追溯了“维特效应”在现代的延续。他的研究表明，在报纸头版刊登自杀报道后，该报道广泛传播地区的自杀率会急剧上升。菲利普斯认为，某些饱受困扰的人在读到他人自杀的新闻后，会模仿他人的行为而自杀。这令人毛骨悚然地体现了社会认同原则：这些人会根据其他饱受困扰的人的行为来决定自己的行为。

Phillips got his evidence for the modern-day Werther effect by examining the suicide statistics in the United States between 1947 and 1968. He found that within two months after every front-page suicide story, an average of fifty-eight more people than usual killed themselves. In a sense, each suicide story killed fifty-eight people who otherwise would have gone on living. Phillips also found that this tendency for suicides to beget suicides occurred principally in those parts of the country where the first suicide was highly publicized and that the wider the publicity given the first suicide, the greater the number of later suicides.

菲利普斯通过研究1947年至1968年间美国的自杀统计数据，找到了现代版“维特效应”的证据。他发现，每篇头版自杀报道刊登后的两个月内，平均会有58人比平时多自杀。从某种意义上说，每篇自杀报道都夺走了58条原本可以活下去的生命。菲利普斯还发现，这种自杀引发更多自杀的趋势主要发生在那些首例自杀事件被大肆报道的地区，而且首例自杀事件的报道范围越广，之后发生的自杀事件就越多。

If the facts surrounding the Werther effect seem to you suspiciously like those surrounding the influence of suicide stories on air and traffic fatalities, the similarities have not been lost on Professor Phillips either. In fact, he contends that all the excess deaths following a front-page suicide incident can be explained as the same thing: copycat suicides. Upon learning of another's suicide, an uncomfortably large number of people decide that suicide is an appropriate action for themselves as well. Some of these individuals then proceed to commit the act in a straightforward, no-bones-about-it fashion, causing the suicide rate to jump.

如果你觉得维特效应的种种迹象与自杀新闻对空难和交通事故死亡人数的影响惊人地相似，那么菲利普斯教授也注意到了其中的关联。事实上，他认为，所有头版自杀事件后出现的超额死亡都可以用同一件事来解释：模仿自杀。当得知他人自杀后，数量惊人的人会认为自杀也是他们自己的选择。这些人中有些会毫不犹豫地付诸行动，导致自杀率飙升。

Others, however, are less direct. For any of several reasons—to protect their reputations, to spare their families the shame and hurt, to allow their dependents to collect on insurance policies—they do not want to appear to have killed themselves. They would rather seem to have died accidentally. So, purposively but furtively, they cause the wreck of a car or a plane they are operating or are simply riding in. This could be accomplished in a variety of all-too-familiar-sounding ways. A commercial-airline pilot could dip the nose of the aircraft at a crucial point of takeoff or could inexplicably land on an already occupied runway against instructions from the control tower; the driver of a car could suddenly swerve into a tree or into oncoming traffic; a passenger in an automobile or corporate jet could incapacitate the operator, causing a deadly crash; the pilot of a private plane could, despite all radio warnings, plow into another aircraft. Thus the alarming climb in crash fatalities we find following front-page suicides is, according to Dr. Phillips, most likely due to the Werther effect secretly applied.

然而，有些人则不那么直接。出于种种原因——为了维护自身名誉，为了避免家人蒙受耻辱和伤害，为了让家属获得保险赔偿——他们不愿承认自己是自杀。他们宁愿看起来像是意外身亡。于是，他们会故意但隐秘地制造自己驾驶或乘坐的汽车或飞机的事故。这种做法有很多种，而且听起来都似曾相识。例如，商业航空公司的飞行员可能在起飞的关键时刻故意降低机头，或者无故违反塔台指令降落在已被占用的跑道上；汽车司机可能突然撞向树木或驶入对向车道；汽车或公务机上的乘客可能使驾驶员失去行动能力，导致致命的坠机事故；私人飞机的飞行员可能无视所有无线电警告，撞向另一架飞机。因此，菲利普斯博士认为，头版自杀事件之后出现的车祸死亡人数惊人地上升，很可能是由于秘密应用了维特效应。

I consider this insight brilliant. First, it explains all of the data beautifully. If these wrecks really are hidden instances of imitative suicide, it makes sense that we should see an increase in the wrecks after suicide stories appear. And it makes sense that the greatest rise in wrecks should occur after the suicide stories that have been most widely publicized and have, consequently, reached the most people. And it makes sense that the number of crashes should jump appreciably only in those geographical areas where the suicide stories were publicized. And it even makes sense that single-victim suicides should lead only to singlevictim crashes, whereas multiple-victim suicide incidents should lead only to multiple-victim crashes. Imitation is the key.

我认为这个见解非常精辟。首先，它完美地解释了所有数据。如果这些车祸真的是模仿自杀的隐蔽案例，那么在自杀事件报道出现后，车祸数量增加就合情合理了。同样合情合理的是，车祸数量增幅最大的事件发生在那些被广泛报道、因此触及范围最广的自杀事件之后。此外，车祸数量显著增加的地区也与自杀事件的报道有关。甚至连单人自杀事件只会导致单人车祸，而多人自杀事件只会导致多人车祸，这些现象也都符合逻辑。模仿是关键所在。

But there is a second valuable feature of Phillips's insight. Not only does it allow us to explain the existing facts, it also allows us to predict new facts that had never been uncovered before. For example, if the abnormally frequent crashes following publicized suicides are genuinely due to imitative rather than accidental actions, they should be more deadly as a result. That is, people trying to kill themselves will likely arrange (with a foot on the accelerator instead of the brake, with the nose of the plane down instead of up) for the impact to be as lethal as possible. The consequence should be quick and sure death. When Phillips examined the records to check on this prediction, he found that the average number of people killed in a fatal crash of a commercial airliner is more than three times greater if the crash happened one week after a front-page suicide story than if it happened one week before. A similar phenomenon can be found in traffic statistics, where there is evidence for the deadly efficiency of postsuicide-story auto crashes. Victims of fatal car wrecks that follow front-page suicide stories die four times more quickly than normal.
