答案令人不安。在与“噩梦”特征完全吻合的情况下，典型的“教师”会竭尽所能地施加痛苦。米尔格拉姆实验中，约三分之二的受试者非但没有理会受害者的恳求，反而拉动了面前三十个电击开关，并持续拉动最后一个开关（450伏），直到研究人员终止实验。更令人震惊的是，这项研究中的四十名受试者，在受害者最初要求释放时，没有一人辞去“教师”的角色；后来，当受害者开始乞求释放时，也没有人辞去；甚至在受害者对每次电击的反应，用米尔格拉姆的话来说，“绝对是痛苦的尖叫”时，也没有人辞去。直到施加了300伏的电击，受害者“绝望地喊叫说他不再回答记忆测试的问题”之后，才有人停止——即便如此，也只是极少数人停止了。

These results surprised everyone associated with the project, Milgram included. In fact, before the study began, he asked groups of colleagues, graduate students, and psychology majors at Yale University (where the experiment was performed) to read a copy of the experimental procedures and estimate how many subjects would go all the way to the last (450-volt) shock. Invariably, the answers fell in the 1 to 2 percent range. A separate group of thirty-nine psychiatrists predicted that only about one person in a thousand would be willing to continue to the end. No one, then, was prepared for the behavior patterns that the experiment actually produced.

这些结果令所有参与该项目的人都感到惊讶，包括米尔格拉姆本人。事实上，在研究开始之前，他曾让耶鲁大学（实验的开展地）的同事、研究生和心理学专业的学生阅读实验流程，并估计有多少受试者会坚持到最后接受450伏的电击。结果几乎无一例外，答案都在1%到2%之间。另一组由39名精神科医生组成的小组预测，大约只有千分之一的人愿意坚持到最后。因此，没有人预料到实验最终会产生这样的行为模式。

How can we explain those alarming patterns? Perhaps, as some have argued, it has to do with the fact that the subjects were all males who are known as a group for their aggressive tendencies, or that the subjects didn't recognize the potential harm that such high shock voltages could cause, or that the subjects were a freakish collection of moral cretins who enjoyed the chance to inflict misery. But there is good evidence against each of these possibilities. First, the subjects' sex was shown by a later experiment to be irrelevant to their willingness to give all the shocks to the victim; female Teachers were just as likely to do so as the males in Milgram's initial study.

我们该如何解释这些令人震惊的模式？或许，正如一些人所认为的那样，这与受试者均为男性有关，而男性群体素来以好斗著称；又或许是因为受试者没有意识到如此高电压电击可能造成的潜在伤害；再或许是因为受试者是一群道德败坏的怪胎，乐于给人带来痛苦。但有充分的证据反驳了这些可能性。首先，后来的实验表明，受试者的性别与他们是否愿意对受害者施加电击无关；在米尔格拉姆最初的研究中，女性教师施加电击的意愿与男性教师一样强烈。

The explanation that subjects weren't aware of the potential physical danger to the victim was also examined in a subsequent experiment and found to be wanting. In that version, when the victim was instructed to announce that he had a heart condition and to declare that his heart was being affected by the shock—"That's all. Get me out of here. I told you I had heart trouble. My heart's starting to bother me. I refuse to go on. Let me out"—the results were the same as before; 65 percent of the subjects carried out their duties faithfully through the maximum shock.

后续实验也检验了受试者未意识到受害者可能面临的身体危险这一解释，结果发现该解释站不住脚。在该实验中，当受试者被指示宣称自己患有心脏病，并表示电击影响了他的心脏——“就这样吧。放我出去。我告诉过你我有心脏病。我的心脏开始不舒服了。我不想继续下去了。放我出去”——结果与之前相同：65%的受试者在遭受最大程度电击的情况下仍然忠实地完成了任务。

Finally, the explanation that Milgram's subjects were a twisted, sadistic bunch not at all representative of the average citizen has proven unsatisfactory as well. The people who answered Milgram's newspaper ad to participate in his "memory" experiment represented a standard cross section of ages, occupations, and educational levels within our society. What's more, later on, a battery of personality scales showed these people to be quite normal psychologically, with not a hint of psychosis as a group. They were, in fact, just like you and me; or, as Milgram likes to term it, they are you and me. If he is right that his studies implicate us in their grisly findings, the unanswered question becomes an uncomfortably personal one: What could make us do such things?

最后，那种认为米尔格拉姆的受试者是一群扭曲、虐待狂，完全不能代表普通民众的解释也同样站不住脚。那些响应米尔格拉姆报纸广告参与其“记忆”实验的人，代表了我们社会中各个年龄段、职业和教育水平的典型人群。更重要的是，之后的一系列人格量表显示，这些人心理状态相当正常，作为一个群体，没有任何精神病的迹象。事实上，他们和我们一样；或者，正如米尔格拉姆喜欢说的那样，他们就是你我。如果他的研究结果确实与我们息息相关，那么未解之谜就变成了一个令人不安的私人问题：究竟是什么驱使我们做出这样的事情？

Milgram is sure he knows the answer. It has to do, he says, with a deep-seated sense of duty to authority within us all. According to Milgram, the real culprit in the experiments was his subject's inability to defy the wishes of the boss of the study—the lab-coated researcher who urged and, if need be, directed the subjects to perform their duties, despite the emotional and physical mayhem they were causing.

米尔格拉姆确信他知道答案。他说，这与我们每个人内心深处根深蒂固的服从权威的意识有关。米尔格拉姆认为，实验中真正的罪魁祸首是他的受试者无法违抗研究负责人的意愿——这位身穿白大褂的研究员敦促，并在必要时指挥受试者完成任务，即便这些任务会造成情感和身体上的混乱。

The evidence supporting Milgram's obedience to authority explanation is strong. First, it is clear that, without the researcher's directives to continue, the subjects would have ended the experiment quickly. They hated what they were doing and agonized over their victim's agony. They implored the researcher to let them stop. When he refused, they went on, but in the process they trembled, they perspired, they shook, they stammered protests and additional pleas for the victim's release. Their fingernails dug into their own flesh; they bit their lips until they bled; they held their heads in their hands; some fell into fits of uncontrollable nervous laughter. As one outside observer to the experiment wrote:

支持米尔格拉姆关于服从权威解释的证据十分有力。首先，很明显，如果没有研究人员的继续指示，受试者会很快结束实验。他们憎恨自己正在做的事情，并为受害者的痛苦而感到痛苦。他们恳求研究人员让他们停止。当研究人员拒绝时，他们继续进行实验，但在这个过程中，他们颤抖、出汗、发抖，结结巴巴地抗议，并再次恳求研究人员释放受害者。他们的指甲深深地嵌入自己的皮肤；他们咬破嘴唇直到流血；他们双手抱头；有些人甚至无法控制地发出神经质的笑声。正如一位实验的外部观察者所写：

I observed a mature and initially poised businessman enter the laboratory smiling and confident. Within twenty minutes he was reduced to a twitching, stuttering wreck who was rapidly approaching a point of nervous collapse. He constantly pulled on his earlobe and twisted his hands. At one point he pushed his fist into his forehead and muttered: "Oh, God, let's stop it." And yet he continued to re 1 spond to every word of the experimenter and obeyed to the end.
我看到一位成熟稳重的商人走进实验室，起初他面带微笑，自信满满。不到二十分钟，他就变得浑身抽搐、结结巴巴，濒临崩溃的边缘。他不停地揪着耳垂，扭动着双手。有一次，他用拳头捶打着额头，喃喃自语：“哦，天哪，停下来吧。”然而，他仍然对实验人员的每一个字都做出回应，一直服从到最后。

In addition to these observations, Milgram has provided even more convincing evidence for the obedience-to-authority interpretation of his subjects' behavior. In a later study, for instance, he had the researcher and the victim switch scripts so that the researcher told the Teacher to stop delivering shocks to the victim, while the victim insisted bravely that the Teacher continue. The result couldn't have been clearer; 100 percent of the subjects refused to give one additional shock when it was merely the fellow subject who demanded it. The identical finding appeared in another version of the experiment in which the researcher and fellow subject switched roles so that it was the researcher who was strapped into the chair and the fellow subject who ordered the Teacher to continue—over the protests of the researcher. Again, not one subject touched another shock lever.

除了这些观察结果之外，米尔格拉姆还提供了更有力的证据，支持对他的受试者行为进行服从权威解释的观点。例如，在后来的研究中，他让研究者和受试者互换角色，由研究者命令“老师”停止对受试者施加电击，而受试者则勇敢地坚持要求“老师”继续。结果显而易见：100%的受试者在仅仅是同伴要求的情况下，都拒绝再施加一次电击。在另一个版本的实验中也出现了相同的结果，在这个版本中，研究者和受试者互换了角色，由研究者被绑在椅子上，而受试者则命令“老师”继续施加电击——尽管研究者提出了抗议。结果依然没有一个受试者触碰过电击杆。

The extreme degree to which subjects in Milgram's situation were attentive to the wishes of authority was documented in yet another variation of the basic study. In this case, Milgram presented the Teacher with two researchers, who issued contradictory orders; one ordered the Teacher to terminate the shocks when the victim cried out for release, while the other maintained that the experiment should go on. These conflicting instructions reliably produced what may have been the project's only humor: In tragicomic befuddlement and with eyes darting from one researcher to another, subjects would beseech the pair to agree on a single command they could follow: "Wait, wait. Which is it going to be? One says stop, one says go. Which is it!?" When the researchers remained at loggerheads, the subjects tried frantically to determine who was the bigger boss. Failing this route to obedience with the authority, every subject finally followed his better instincts and ended the shocks. As in the other experimental variations, such a result would hardly be expected had the subjects' motivations involved some form of sadism or neurotic aggressiveness.

米尔格拉姆实验中受试者对权威指令的极度服从，在另一项类似实验中也得到了证实。在这个实验中，米尔格拉姆安排了两位研究人员分别向“老师”下达相互矛盾的指令：一位研究人员命令“老师”在“老师”发出停止电击的呼喊时停止电击，而另一位研究人员则坚持实验应该继续进行。这些相互冲突的指令产生了可能是整个实验中唯一的幽默之处：受试者们在一种悲喜剧般的困惑中，目光在两位研究人员之间来回游移，恳求他们达成一致，制定一个可以执行的指令：“等等，等等。到底哪个指令有效？一个说停，一个说继续。到底哪个指令有效！？”当两位研究人员意见不一时，受试者们便疯狂地试图弄清楚谁才是真正的权威。在无法通过这种方式获得服从后，每个受试者最终都遵循了自己的直觉，停止了电击。与其他实验变体一样，如果受试者的动机涉及某种形式的虐待狂或神经质的攻击性，那么这样的结果几乎是不可能出现的。

To Milgram's mind, evidence of a chilling phenomenon emerges repeatedly from his accumulated data: "It is the extreme willingness of adults to go to almost any lengths on the command of an authority that constitutes the chief finding of the study." There are sobering implications of this finding for those concerned about the ability of another form of authority—government—to extract frightening levels of obedience from ordinary citizens. Furthermore, the finding tells us something about the sheer strength of authority pressures in controlling our behavior. After witnessing Milgram's subjects squirming and sweating and suffering at their task, could anyone doubt the power of the force that held them there?

在米尔格拉姆看来，他积累的数据反复揭示了一种令人不寒而栗的现象：“成年人为了服从权威，几乎愿意付出任何代价，这构成了这项研究的主要发现。”对于那些担忧另一种权威形式——政府——能否从普通公民身上榨取令人恐惧的服从的人来说，这一发现具有令人警醒的意义。此外，这一发现也揭示了权威压力在控制我们行为方面的巨大威力。目睹米尔格拉姆的受试者在执行任务时扭动身体、汗流浃背、痛苦不堪，还有谁会怀疑维系他们的力量呢？

For those whose doubts remain, the story of S. Brian Willson might prove instructive. On September 1, 1987, to protest U.S. shipments of military equipment to Nicaragua, Mr. Willson and two other men stretched their bodies across the railroad tracks leading out of the Concord, California, Naval Weapons Station. The protesters were confident that their act would halt the scheduled train's progress that day, as they had notified Navy and railroad officials of their intent three days before. But the civilian crew, which had been given orders not to stop, never even slowed the train, despite being able to see the protesters six hundred feet ahead. Although two of the men managed to scramble out of harm's way, Mr. Willson was not quick enough to avoid being struck and having both legs severed below the knee. Because Navy medical corpsmen at the scene refused to treat him or allow him to be taken to the hospital in their ambulance, onlookers—including Mr. Willson's wife and son—were left to try to stanch the flow of blood for forty-five minutes until a private ambulance arrived.

对于那些仍有疑虑的人来说，S·布莱恩·威尔逊的故事或许能起到警示作用。1987年9月1日，为了抗议美国向尼加拉瓜运送军事装备，威尔逊先生和另外两名男子横卧在加利福尼亚州康科德海军武器站外的铁轨上。抗议者们自信他们的行动能够阻止当天预定的列车通行，因为他们三天前就已通知了海军和铁路官员他们的意图。然而，尽管接到不得停车命令的平民乘务员能够看到前方600英尺处的抗议者，却丝毫没有减速。虽然其中两名男子设法躲开了，但威尔逊先生却没能及时避开，被火车撞击，双腿膝盖以下被截断。由于现场的海军医务兵拒绝为他治疗，也不允许用他们的救护车将他送往医院，围观者——包括威尔逊先生的妻子和儿子——只能设法止血 45 分钟，直到一辆私人救护车到达。

Amazingly, Mr. Willson, who served four years in Vietnam, does not blame either the crewmen or the corpsmen for his misfortune; he points his finger, instead, at a system that constrained their actions through the pressure to obey: "They were just doing what I did in 'Nam. They were following orders that are part of an insane policy. They're the fall guys." Although the crew members shared Mr. Willson's assessment of them as victims, they did not share his magnanimity. In what is perhaps the most remarkable aspect of the incident, the train crew filed suit against him, requesting punitive damages for the "humiliation, mental anguish, and physical stress" they suffered because he hadn't allowed them to carry out their orders without cutting off his legs.

令人惊讶的是，曾在越南服役四年的威尔逊先生并没有将自己的不幸归咎于列车员或医护兵；相反，他将矛头指向了那个通过强制服从来限制他们行动的体制：“他们只是在做我在越南做过的事。他们执行的命令是荒谬政策的一部分。他们是替罪羊。”尽管列车员们也认同威尔逊先生对他们的受害者身份，但他们并不像他那样宽宏大量。或许这起事件最令人震惊之处在于，列车员们起诉了他，要求他赔偿因“羞辱、精神痛苦和身体压力”而遭受的惩罚性赔偿，因为他不允许他们在不砍断自己双腿的情况下执行命令。

Whenever we are faced with so potent a motivator of human action, it is natural to expect that good reasons exist for the motivation. In the case of obedience to authority, even a brief consideration of human social organization offers justification aplenty. A multilayered and widely accepted system of authority confers an immense advantage upon a society. It allows the development of sophisticated structures for resource production, trade, defense, expansion, and social control that would otherwise be impossible. The other alternative, anarchy, is a state that is hardly known for its beneficial effects on cultural groups and one that the social philosopher Thomas Hobbes assures us would render life "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." Consequently, we are trained from birth that obedience to proper authority is right and disobedience is wrong. The essential message fills the parental lessons, the schoolhouse rhymes, stories, and songs of our childhood and is carried forward in the legal, military, and political systems we encounter as adults. Notions of submission and loyalty to legitimate rule are accorded much value in each.

每当我们面对如此强大的人类行为动机时，自然会期望其背后存在充分的理由。就服从权威而言，即使只是对人类社会组织稍作思考，也能找到诸多合理的解释。一个多层次且被广泛接受的权威体系能为社会带来巨大的优势。它使得资源生产、贸易、国防、扩张和社会控制等复杂结构的建立成为可能，而这些在其他情况下是无法实现的。另一种选择是无政府状态，这种状态几乎不会对文化群体产生任何益处，社会哲学家托马斯·霍布斯曾断言，无政府状态会使生活变得“孤独、贫穷、肮脏、野蛮而短暂”。因此，我们从出生起就被灌输服从权威是正确的，不服从权威是错误的观念。这一核心信息贯穿于我们童年时期父母的教诲、学校的童谣、故事和歌曲，并在我们成年后所接触的法律、军事和政治体系中得以延续。在每一种情况下，服从和忠于合法统治的观念都备受重视。

Religious instruction contributes as well. The very first book of the Bible, for example, describes how failure to obey the ultimate authority produced the loss of paradise for Adam, Eve, and the rest of the human race. Should that particular metaphor prove too subtle, just a bit further into the Old Testament we can read—in what might be the closest biblical representation of the Milgram experiment—the respectful account of Abraham's willingness to plunge a dagger through the heart of his young son, because God, without any explanation, ordered it. We learn it this story that the correctness of an action was not adjudged by such considerations as apparent senselessness, harmfulness, injustice, or usual moral standards, but by the mere command of a higher authority. Abraham's tormented ordeal was a test of obedience, and he—like Milgram's subjects, who perhaps had learned an early lesson from him—passed.

宗教教义也起到了一定的作用。例如，《圣经》的第一卷就描述了亚当、夏娃以及全人类因不服从至高权威而失去伊甸园的悲剧。如果这个比喻过于隐晦，我们不妨再翻阅一下旧约，或许能找到与米尔格拉姆实验最接近的圣经版本——亚伯拉罕甘愿将匕首刺入幼子心脏的故事，因为上帝没有给出任何解释，就下达了这样的命令。这个故事告诉我们，判断一个行为是否正确，并非基于表面上的无意义、有害、不公或通常的道德标准，而仅仅是出于更高权威的命令。亚伯拉罕所遭受的痛苦考验是对他服从的考验，而他——就像米尔格拉姆的实验对象一样，或许他们早早就从亚伯拉罕身上学到了教训——通过了考验。

Stories like those of Abraham and Milgram's subjects can tell us much about the power of and value for obedience in our culture. In another sense, however, they may be misleading as to the way obedience typically occurs. We rarely agonize to such a degree over the pros and cons of authority's demands. In fact, our obedience frequently takes place in a click, whirr fashion, with little or no conscious deliberation. Information from a recognized authority can provide us a valuable shortcut for deciding how to act in a situation.

像亚伯拉罕和米尔格拉姆实验对象的故事，可以让我们深入了解服从在我们文化中的力量和价值。然而，从另一个角度来看，这些故事也可能误导我们对服从通常发生方式的理解。我们很少会如此纠结于权威要求的利弊。事实上，我们的服从往往是下意识的、机械式的，几乎没有经过深思熟虑。来自权威人士的信息可以为我们提供一个快速决策的捷径，帮助我们决定在特定情况下应该如何行动。

After all, as Milgram himself suggests, conforming to the dictates of authority figures has always had genuine practical advantages for us. Early on, these people (for example, parents, teachers) knew more than we did, and we found that taking their advice proved beneficial—partly because of their greater wisdom and partly because they controlled our rewards and punishments. As adults, the same benefits persist for the same reasons, though the authority figures now appear as employers, judges, and government leaders. Because their positions speak of superior access to information and power, it makes great sense to comply with the wishes of properly constituted authorities. It makes so much sense, in fact, that we often do so when it makes no sense at all.

毕竟，正如米尔格拉姆本人所言，服从权威人士的指示一直以来都对我们有着切实的好处。在孩提时代，这些人（例如父母、老师）比我们懂得更多，我们发现听从他们的建议是有益的——部分原因是他们拥有更丰富的智慧，部分原因是他们掌控着我们的奖惩。成年后，出于同样的原因，这些好处依然存在，尽管权威人士如今变成了雇主、法官和政府领导人。由于他们的地位意味着拥有更优越的信息获取渠道和权力，因此服从合法权威人士的意愿就显得合情合理。事实上，这种做法如此合情合理，以至于我们常常在完全没有道理的情况下也照做。

This paradox is, of course, the same one that attends all major weapons of influence. In this instance, once we realize that obedience to authority is mostly rewarding, it is easy to allow ourselves the convenience of automatic obedience. The simultaneous blessing and bane of such blind obedience is its mechanical character. We don't have to think; therefore, we don't. Although such mindless obedience leads us to appropriate action in the great majority of cases, there will be conspicuous exceptions—because we are reacting rather than thinking.

当然，这种悖论也同样存在于所有主要的权力工具之中。在这种情况下，一旦我们意识到服从权威大多时候是有益的，就很容易让自己陷入自动服从的便利之中。这种盲目服从的利弊就在于它的机械性。我们不必思考；因此，我们也就不思考了。虽然这种不假思索的服从在绝大多数情况下都能引导我们采取恰当的行动，但总会有一些明显的例外——因为我们是在做出反应，而不是在思考。

Let's take an example from one facet of our lives where authority pressures are visible and strong: medicine. Health is enormously important to us. Thus, physicians, who possess large amounts of knowledge and influence in this vital area, hold the position of respected authorities. In addition, the medical establishment has a clearly terraced power and prestige structure. The various kinds of health workers well understand the level of their jobs in this structure; and they well understand, too, that the M.D. sits at the top. No one may overrule the doctor's judgment in a case, except perhaps, another doctor of higher rank. As a consequence, a long-established tradition of automatic obedience to a doctor's orders has developed among health-care staffs.

让我们以生活中权威压力显而易见且影响深远的一个领域——医疗——为例。健康对我们至关重要。因此，在这个至关重要的领域拥有丰富知识和巨大影响力的医生，享有崇高的权威地位。此外，医疗体系拥有清晰的权力与声望层级结构。各类医务人员都清楚自己在这一结构中的职位级别；他们也深知，医学博士（M.D.）处于最高层。除了级别更高的医生之外，任何人不得推翻医生的诊断。因此，医务人员中逐渐形成了一种根深蒂固的、对医生指令绝对服从的传统。

The worrisome possibility arises, then, that when a physician makes a clear error, no one lower in the hierarchy will think to question it—precisely because, once a legitimate authority has given an order, subordinates stop thinking in the situation and start reacting. Mix this kind of click, whirr response into a complex hospital environment and mistakes are certain. Indeed a study done in the early 1980s by the U.S. Health Care Financing Administration showed that, for patient medication alone, the average hospital had a 12 percent daily error rate. A decade later, things had not improved: According to a Harvard University study, 10 percent of all cardiac arrests in hospitals are attributable to medication errors. Errors in the medicine patients receive can occur for a variety of reasons. However, a book entitled Medication Errors: Causes and Prevention by two Temple University pharmacology professors, Michael Cohen and Neil Davis, attributes much of the problem to the mindless deference given the "boss" of the patient's case: the attending physician. According to Professor Cohen, "in case after case, patients, nurses, pharmacists, and other physicians do not question the prescription." Take, for example, the strange case of the "rectal earache" reported by Cohen and Davis. A physician ordered ear drops to be administered to the right ear of a patient suffering pain and infection there. But instead of writing out completely the location "right ear" on the prescription, the doctor abbreviated it so that the instructions read "place in R ear." Upon receiving the prescription, the duty nurse promptly put the required number of ear drops into the patient's anus.

因此，令人担忧的可能性是，当医生犯下明显的错误时，层级较低的人可能不会提出质疑——正是因为一旦合法权威下达指令，下属就会停止思考，开始被动反应。在复杂的医院环境中，这种机械式的反应必然会导致错误。事实上，美国医疗保健融资管理局在20世纪80年代初进行的一项研究表明，仅就患者用药而言，医院平均每天的错误率就高达12%。十年后，情况并未好转：哈佛大学的一项研究显示，医院所有心脏骤停病例中有10%是由用药错误造成的。患者用药错误可能由多种原因引起。然而，坦普尔大学药理学教授迈克尔·科恩和尼尔·戴维斯合著的《用药错误：原因与预防》一书指出，造成这一问题的主要原因是人们对负责患者病情的“老板”——主治医生——的盲目服从。科恩教授指出，“在很多案例中，患者、护士、药剂师和其他医生都不会质疑处方。”例如，科恩和戴维斯报告的“直肠耳痛”这一奇特案例。一位医生给一位右耳疼痛且有感染的患者开了耳药水。但医生并没有在处方上完整写出“右耳”，而是缩写为“置于右耳”。值班护士收到处方后，立即将所需剂量的耳药水注入了患者的肛门。

Obviously, rectal treatment of an earache made no sense. Yet neither the patient nor the nurse questioned it. The important lesson of this story is that in many situations where a legitimate authority has spoken, what would otherwise make sense is irrelevant. In these instances, we don't consider the situation as a whole but attend and respond to only one aspect of it.

显然，用直肠治疗耳痛是毫无道理的。然而，病人和护士都没有质疑。这个故事的重要教训是，在许多情况下，当权威人士发表意见时，原本看似合理的做法就变得无关紧要了。在这种情况下，我们没有从整体上考虑问题，而只是关注并回应其中的某个方面。

Wherever our behaviors are governed in such an unthinking manner, we can be confident that there will be compliance professionals trying to take advantage. We can stay within the field of medicine and see that advertisers have frequently harnessed the respect accorded to doctors in our culture by hiring actors to play the roles of doctors speaking on behalf of the product. My favorite example is a TV commercial featuring actor Robert Young counseling people against the dangers of caffeine and recommending caffeine-free Sanka Brand coffee. The commercial was highly successful, selling so much coffee that it was played for years in several versions. But why should this commercial prove so effective? Why on earth would we take Robert Young's word for the health consequences of decaffeinated coffee? Because—as the advertising agency that hired him knew perfectly well—he is associated in the minds of the American public with Marcus Welby, M.D., the role he played in an earlier long-running television series. Objectively it doesn't make sense to be swayed by the comments of a man we know to be just an actor who used to play a doctor. But, as a practical matter, that man moved the Sanka.

凡是我们的行为被如此不假思索地支配的地方，我们都可以确信，总会有合规专家试图从中牟利。以医疗领域为例，广告商经常利用人们文化中对医生的尊重，聘请演员扮演医生，为产品代言。我最喜欢的例子是一则电视广告，演员罗伯特·杨在广告中劝告人们不要摄入咖啡因，并推荐不含咖啡因的Sanka牌咖啡。这则广告非常成功，咖啡销量惊人，以至于多年来以多个版本反复播放。但为什么这则广告如此有效？我们为什么要相信罗伯特·杨关于无咖啡因咖啡对健康影响的说法？因为——正如聘请他的广告公司非常清楚的那样——在美国公众的印象中，他与马库斯·韦尔比医生联系在一起，这是他早年在一部长寿电视剧中扮演的角色。客观地说，被一个我们知道只是曾经扮演过医生的演员的话所左右，是毫无道理的。但实际上，那个人移动了桑卡号。

# ↩

CONNOTATION, NOT CONTENT

含义，而非内容

From the first time I saw it, the most intriguing feature for me in the Robert Young Sanka commercial was its ability to use the influence of the authority principle without ever providing a real authority. The appearance of authority was enough. This tells us something important about unthinking reactions to authority figures. When in a click, whirr mode, we are often as vulnerable to the symbols of authority as to the substance.

我第一次看到罗伯特·杨为Sanka拍摄的广告时，最吸引我的就是它巧妙地运用了权威原则，却从未真正赋予任何权威。仅仅是权威的表象就足以打动人心。这揭示了我们对权威人物不假思索的反应中一个重要的问题。当我们处于一种“咔哒咔哒”的快节奏状态时，我们往往既容易受到权威象征的影响，也容易受到权威本身的影响。

There are several kinds of symbols that can reliably trigger our compliance in the absence of the genuine substance of authority. Consequently, they are employed extensively by those compliance professionals who are short on substance. Con artists, for example, drape themselves with the titles, clothes, and trappings of authority. They love nothing more than to emerge elegantly dressed from a fine automobile and to introduce themselves to their prospective "mark" as Doctor or Judge or Professor or Commissioner Someone. They understand that when they are so equipped, their chances for compliance are greatly increased. Each of these three types of symbols of authority has its own story and is worth a separate look.

在缺乏真正权威的情况下，有几种符号可以有效地诱使我们服从。因此，那些缺乏实质内容的合规专家会广泛使用这些符号。例如，骗子会把自己包装成权威人士，并穿戴相应的头衔、服饰和各种装束。他们最喜欢的就是衣着光鲜地从一辆豪华轿车中走出来，向他们的潜在“目标”介绍自己是医生、法官、教授或某某专员。他们明白，一旦拥有了这些“装备”，他们获得服从的机会就会大大增加。这三种权威符号各有其故事，值得分别探讨。

Titles

标题

Titles are simultaneously the most difficult and the easiest symbols of authority to acquire. To earn one normally takes years of work and achievement. Yet it is possible for somebody who has put in none of this effort to adopt the mere label and receive a kind of automatic deference. As we have seen, TV-commercial actors and con artists do it successfully all the time.

头衔既是最难获得的权威象征，也是最容易获得的权威象征。通常，获得一个头衔需要多年的努力和成就。然而，有些人无需付出任何努力，仅仅凭借一个头衔就能自动获得某种程度的尊重。正如我们所见，电视广告演员和骗子们经常成功地做到这一点。

I recently talked with a friend—a faculty member at a well-known eastern university—who provided a telling illustration of how our actions are frequently more influenced by a title than by the nature of the person claiming it. My friend travels quite a bit and often finds himself chatting with strangers in bars, restaurants, and airports. He says that he has learned through much experience never to use his title—profess-or—during these conversations. When he does, he reports, the tenor of the interaction changes immediately. People who have been spontaneous and interesting conversation partners for the prior half hour become respectful, accepting, and dull. His opinions that earlier might have produced a lively exchange now usually generate extended (and highly grammatical) statements of accord. Annoyed and slightly bewildered by the phenomenon—because, as he says, "I'm still the same guy they've been talking to for the past thirty minutes, right?"—my friend now regularly lies about his occupation in such situations.

我最近和一位朋友聊天，他是一位在东部知名大学任教的教授。他举了一个很有说服力的例子，说明我们的行为往往更多地受到头衔的影响，而不是头衔持有者本身的特质。我的朋友经常出差，也经常在酒吧、餐厅和机场与陌生人聊天。他说，他从多年的经验中学到，在这些对话中绝不使用自己的头衔——教授或教授。他说，一旦使用了头衔，对话的气氛就会立刻改变。之前半小时里，那些和他谈吐风趣、妙语连珠的人，现在会变得彬彬有礼、不以为然，但却索然无味。他之前可能引发热烈讨论的观点，现在通常只会换来对方冗长（且语法严谨）的附和。我的朋友对这种现象感到恼火又有些困惑——因为正如他所说，“我还是他们过去半小时一直在跟我聊天的那个人，对吧？”——所以现在，在这种情况下，他通常会谎报自己的职业。

What a refreshing shift from the more typical pattern in which certain compliance practitioners lie about titles they don't truly have. In either direction, however, such practiced dishonesty makes the same point about the sufficiency of a mere symbol of authority to influence behavior.

这与某些合规从业人员谎报职称的常见做法截然不同，令人耳目一新。然而，无论哪种情况，这种惯于撒谎的行为都表明，仅仅依靠权威的象征就能左右人们的行为。

I wonder whether my professor friend—who is physically somewhat short—would be so eager to hide his title if he knew that, besides making strangers more accommodating, it also makes them see him as taller. Studies investigating the way in which authority status affects perceptions of size have found that prestigious titles lead to height distortions. In one experiment conducted on five classes of Australian college students, a man was introduced as a visitor from Cambridge University in England. However, his status at Cambridge was represented differently in each of the classes. To one class, he was presented as a student; to a second class, a demonstrator; to another, a lecturer; to yet another, a senior lecturer; to a fifth, a professor. After he left the room, each class was asked to estimate his height. It was found that with each increase in status, the same man grew in perceived height by an average of a half inch, so that as the "professor" he was seen as two and a half inches taller than as the "student."

我很好奇，如果我那位身高略矮的教授朋友知道，除了让陌生人更友好之外，他的头衔还能让他们觉得他更高，他还会如此急于隐藏自己的头衔吗？一些研究探讨了权威地位如何影响人们对身高的感知，结果发现，显赫的头衔会导致身高错觉。在一项针对澳大利亚五大班大学生的实验中，一位男士被介绍为来自英国剑桥大学的访客。然而，他在每个班级的身份描述都不同。在一个班级里，他被介绍为学生；在另一个班级里，他是助教；在另一个班级里，他是讲师；在另一个班级里，他是高级讲师；在第五个班级里，他是教授。他离开教室后，每个班级都被要求估计他的身高。结果发现，随着身份的提升，这位男士在人们眼中的身高平均增加了半英寸，因此，作为“教授”的他比作为“学生”时看起来高出两英寸半。

It is worth the time of a small detour to pursue this interesting connection between status and perceived size, since it shows up in a variety of ways. In judging the size of coins, for example, children most overestimate the size of the more valuable coins. And adults are just as guilty of such distortions. In one study, college students drew cards that had monetary values printed on them ranging from $3.00 to -$3.00; they won or lost the amount shown on the cards they picked. Afterward, they were asked to rate the size of each card. Even though all cards were exactly the same size, those that had the more extreme values—positive or negative—were seen as physically larger. Thus it is not necessarily the pleasantness of a thing that makes it seem bigger to us, it is its importance. 6

值得花点时间探讨一下地位与感知大小之间的这种有趣联系，因为它以多种方式体现出来。例如，在判断硬币大小时，孩子们往往会高估面值更高的硬币的大小。成年人也同样会犯这种认知偏差。在一项研究中，大学生们抽取卡片，卡片上印有从 3 美元到 -3 美元不等的金额；他们根据抽到的卡片上的金额进行赢或输。之后，研究人员要求他们对每张卡片的大小进行评分。尽管所有卡片的实际大小完全相同，但那些金额更极端（正数或负数）的卡片看起来却更大。因此，让我们觉得某物更大的，并非是它的愉悦感，而是它的重要性。

Because we see size and status as related, it is possible for certain individuals to benefit by substituting the former for the latter. In some animal societies, where the status of a male is assigned on the basis of dominance, size is an important factor in determining which male will achieve which status level in the group. 7 Usually, in combat with a rival, the larger and more powerful male wins. To avoid the harmful effects to the group of such physical conflict, however, many species have adopted methods that frequently involve more form than fracas. The two males confront each other with showy aggression displays that invariably include size-enhancing tricks. Various mammals arch their backs and bristle their coats; fish extend their fins and puff themselves up with water; birds unfurl and flutter their wings. Very often, this exhibition alone is enough to send one of the histrionic warriors into retreat, leaving the contested status position to his seemingly larger and stronger rival.

由于我们认为体型和地位相关，某些个体有可能通过以体型取代地位而获益。在一些动物社会中，雄性的地位取决于其支配地位，体型是决定雄性在群体中地位的重要因素。通常情况下，在与竞争对手的争斗中，体型更大、力量更强的雄性会获胜。然而，为了避免这种肢体冲突对群体造成的伤害，许多物种采取了更多形式而非实际冲突的策略。两只雄性会通过炫耀性的攻击行为来互相对抗，这些行为通常包含一些增强体型的技巧。各种哺乳动物会拱起背部，竖起毛发；鱼类会伸展鳍，并吸水膨胀身体；鸟类会展开并扇动翅膀。很多时候，仅仅是这种展示就足以让其中一只爱出风头的雄性退却，从而将争夺的地位拱手让给看起来体型更大、力量更强的竞争对手。

Fur, fins, and feathers. Isn't it interesting how these most delicate of parts can be exploited to give the impression of substance and weight? There are two lessons for us here. One is specific to the association between size and status. The connection of those two things can be profitably employed by individuals who are able to fake the first to gain the appearance of the second. This is precisely why con men, even those of average or slightly above-average height, commonly wear lifts in their shoes.

皮毛、鳍和羽毛。这些最娇嫩的部位竟能被用来营造厚重感，这难道不令人惊叹吗？这里蕴含着两点启示。其一是体型与地位之间的关联。有些人能够伪造体型，从而获得地位，而这种关联正是他们牟利的法宝。这就是为什么骗子，即便身高一般或略高于平均水平，也常常会在鞋里垫增高垫的原因。

The other lesson is more general: The outward signs of power and authority frequently may be counterfeited with the flimsiest of materials. Let's return to the realm of titles for an example—an example that involves what, in several ways, is the scariest experiment I know. A group of researchers, composed of doctors and nurses with connections to three midwestern hospitals, became increasingly concerned with the extent of mechanical obedience to doctors' orders on the part of nurses. It seemed to the researchers that even highly trained and skilled nurses were not using that training or skill sufficiently to check on a doctor's judgment; instead, when confronted with a physician's directives, they would simply defer.

另一个教训更为普遍：权力和权威的外在标志往往可以用最薄弱的材料伪造。让我们回到头衔的领域，举个例子——这个例子涉及我所知的最令人毛骨悚然的实验。一组由医生和护士组成的研究人员，与美国中西部三家医院有联系，他们越来越关注护士对医生指令的机械服从程度。研究人员发现，即使是训练有素、技能娴熟的护士，也没有充分利用他们的训练或技能来质疑医生的判断；相反，当面对医生的指示时，她们只是简单地服从。

Earlier, we saw how this process accounted for the case of the rectally administered ear drops. But the midwestern researchers took things several steps further. First, they wanted to find out whether such cases were isolated incidents or representative of a widespread phenomenon. Second, they wanted to examine the problem in the context of a serious treatment error—the gross overprescription of an unauthorized drug to a hospital patient. Finally, they wanted to see what would happen if they physically removed the authority figure from the situation and substituted an unfamiliar voice on the phone, offering only the frailest evidence of authority—the claimed title "doctor."

之前我们已经了解了这一过程如何解释了直肠给药滴耳液的案例。但中西部的研究人员更进一步。首先，他们想弄清楚这类案例是孤立事件还是普遍现象。其次，他们想在一个严重的医疗事故——给住院病人过度开具未经授权的药物——的背景下审视这个问题。最后，他们想看看，如果他们将权威人物从现场移除，换成一个陌生人通过电话联系，而对方仅提供最薄弱的权威证明——自称“医生”——会发生什么。

To twenty-two separate nurses' stations on various surgical, medical, pediatric, and psychiatric wards, one of the researchers made an identical phone call in which he identified himself as a hospital physician and directed the answering nurse to give twenty milligrams of a drug (Astrogen) to a specific ward patient. There were four excellent reasons for a nurse's caution in response to this order: (1) The prescription was transmitted by phone, in direct violation of hospital policy. (2) The medication itself was unauthorized; Astrogen had not been cleared for use nor placed on the ward stock list. (3) The prescribed dosage was obviously and dangerously excessive. The medication containers clearly stated that the "maximum daily dose" was only ten milligrams, half of what had been ordered. (4) The directive was given by a man the nurse had never met, seen, or even talked with before on the phone. Yet, in 95 percent of the instances, the nurses went straightaway to the ward medicine cabinet, where they secured the ordered dosage of Astrogen and started for the patient's room to administer it. It was at this point that they were stopped by a secret observer, who revealed the nature of the experiment.

研究人员分别致电22个位于不同外科、内科、儿科和精神科病房的护士站，拨打相同的电话。他在电话中自称是医院医生，并指示接听电话的护士给一位特定病房的病人服用20毫克的药物（阿司匹林）。护士对这一指令保持谨慎，原因有四：（1）处方是通过电话传达的，直接违反了医院的规定。（2）该药物本身未经授权；阿司匹林既未获得使用许可，也未列入病房的药品清单。（3）处方剂量明显过高，存在危险。药品包装上明确标明“每日最大剂量”仅为10毫克，是处方剂量的一半。（4）发出指令的人是护士从未见过、甚至从未通过电话交谈过的男子。然而，在95%的情况下，护士们直接前往病房药柜，取出所需剂量的阿司匹林，然后前往病房给病人服用。就在这时，她们被一名秘密观察员拦住，观察员揭露了实验的真相。

The results are frightening, indeed. That 95 percent of regular staff nurses complied unhesitatingly with a patently improper instruction of this sort must give us all great reason for concern as potential hospital patients. Given the recent U.S. Health Care Financing Administration estimate of a 12 percent daily-medication error rate in American hospitals, stays of longer than a week make it likely that we will be recipients of such an error. What the midwestern study shows is that the mistakes are hardly limited to trivial slips in the administration of harmless ear drops or the like, but extend to grave and dangerous blunders.

结果确实令人震惊。95%的普通护士毫不犹豫地执行了这种明显错误的指令，这无疑让我们所有潜在的住院患者都感到担忧。鉴于美国医疗保健融资管理局最近估计美国医院的每日用药错误率高达12%，住院超过一周就意味着我们很可能成为此类错误的受害者。这项来自中西部的研究表明，这些错误绝不仅仅是给患者滴耳液等无害药物时出现的小失误，而是会造成严重且危险的后果。

In interpreting their unsettling findings, the researchers came to an instructive conclusion:

在解读这些令人不安的发现时，研究人员得出了一个富有启发性的结论：

In a real-life situation corresponding to the experimental one, there would, in theory, be two professional intelligences, the doctor's and the nurse's, working to ensure that a given procedure be undertaken in a manner beneficial to the patient or, at the very least, not detrimental to him. The experiment strongly suggests, however, that one of these intelligences is, for all practical purposes, nonfunctioning.
在与实验情境相对应的现实情境中，理论上应该存在两种专业智能——医生和护士的智能——共同协作，以确保特定医疗程序以对患者有利或至少不有害的方式进行。然而，实验结果强烈表明，其中一种智能实际上已经失效。

It seems that, in the face of a physician's directives, the nurses unhooked their "professional intelligences" and moved to a click, whirr form of responding. None of their considerable medical training or knowledge was engaged in the decision of what to do. Instead, because obedience to legitimate authority had always been the most preferred and efficient action in their work setting, they had become willing to err on the side of automatic obedience. It is all the more instructive that they had traveled so far in this direction that their error had come not in response to genuine authority but to its most easily falsified sym-bol—a bare title.

面对医生的指示，护士们似乎放弃了她们的“专业智慧”，转而采取机械式的反应模式。她们丰富的医学训练和知识完全没有参与决策。相反，由于在她们的工作环境中，服从合法权威一直是她们最首选、最有效的做法，她们便甘愿盲目服从。更令人深思的是，她们在这方面走得太远，以至于她们的错误并非源于对真正权威的服从，而是源于对权威最容易被伪造的象征——一个空洞的头衔——的盲目服从。

Clothes

衣服

A second kind of authority symbol that can trigger our mechanical compliance is clothing. Though more tangible than a title, the cloak of authority is every bit as fakable. Police bunco files bulge with records of con artists whose artistry includes the quick change. In chameleon style, they adopt the hospital white, priestly black, army green, or police blue that the situation requires for maximum advantage. Only too late do their victims realize that the garb of authority is hardly its guarantee.

第二种能让我们机械服从的权威象征是服饰。虽然比头衔更具体，但这种权威的伪装同样容易造假。警方的诈骗档案里充斥着骗子的记录，他们的绝技之一就是快速换装。他们像变色龙一样，根据不同的场合，换上医院的白色、牧师的黑色、军绿色或警蓝色等各种颜色的衣服，以达到最大的欺骗效果。受害者往往要到为时已晚才会意识到，权威的外衣并不能保证真正的权威。

A series of studies by social psychologist Leonard Bickman gives an indication of how difficult it can be to resist requests that come from figures in authority attire. Bickman's basic procedure was to ask pass-ersby on the street to comply with some sort of odd request (to pick up a discarded paper bag, to stand on the other side of a bus-stop sign). In half of the instances, the requester—a young man—was dressed in normal street clothes; the rest of the time, he was dressed in a security guard's uniform. Regardless of the type of request, many more people obeyed the requester when he wore the guard costume.

社会心理学家伦纳德·比克曼的一系列研究表明，人们很难拒绝身着权威服饰的人提出的要求。比克曼的基本方法是，在街上随机询问路人一些看似奇怪的请求（例如捡起一个被丢弃的纸袋，或者站在公交车站牌的另一侧）。其中一半情况下，提出请求的人——一位年轻男子——穿着普通的便服；另一半情况下，他则穿着保安制服。无论请求的内容是什么，当请求者身穿保安制服时，更多的人会服从他的请求。

Especially revealing was one version of the experiment in which the requester stopped pedestrians and pointed to a man standing by a parking meter fifty feet away. The requester, whether dressed normally or as a security guard, always said the same thing to the pedestrian: "You see that guy over there by the meter? He's overparked but doesn't have any change. Give him a dime!" The requester then turned a corner and walked away so that by the time the pedestrian reached the meter, the requester was out of sight. The power of his uniform lasted, however, even after he was long gone: Nearly all the pedestrians complied with his directive when he had worn the guard costume, but fewer than half did so when he had dressed normally. It is interesting to note that later on, Bickman found college students able to guess with considerable accuracy the percentage of compliance that had occurred in the experiment when the requester wore street clothes (50 percent vs. the actual 42 percent); yet the students greatly underestimated the percentage of compliance when he was in uniform (63 percent vs. the actual 92 percent). 10

尤其引人注目的是其中一个实验版本：请求者拦住行人，指着五十英尺外停车计时器旁站着的一个人。无论请求者穿着便服还是保安制服，他总是对行人说同样的话：“你看到那边计时器旁的那个人了吗？他停车超时了，但没零钱。给他一角钱吧！”说完，请求者便转身离开，等行人走到计时器旁时，他已经不见踪影。然而，他的制服威慑力却在他离开很久之后依然存在：当他穿着保安制服时，几乎所有行人都会照做；而当他穿着便服时，只有不到一半的行人会照做。值得注意的是，后来比克曼发现，大学生们能够相当准确地猜出请求者穿着便服时，行人照做的比例（50% vs. 实际的42%）。然而，学生们大大低估了他在穿制服时的服从率（63% 对比实际的 92%）。

Less blatant in its connotation than a uniform, but nonetheless effective, is another kind of attire that has traditionally bespoken authority status in our culture: the well-tailored business suit. It, too, can evoke a telling form of deference from total strangers. Research conducted in Texas, for instance, arranged for a thirty-one-year-old man to violate the law by crossing the street against the traffic light on a variety of occasions. In half of the cases, he was dressed in a freshly pressed business suit and tie; on the other occasions, he wore a work shirt and trousers. The researchers watched from a distance and counted the number of pedestrians waiting at the corner who followed the man across the street. Like the children of Hamelin who crowded after the Pied Piper, three and a half times as many people swept into traffic behind the suited jaywalker. In this case, though, the magic came not from his pipe but his pinstripes. 11

虽然其象征意义不如制服那样直白，但同样有效的还有另一种在我们的文化中历来具有权威象征意义的着装：剪裁合身的商务套装。它也能唤起陌生人某种意味深长的敬意。例如，德克萨斯州的一项研究安排一位31岁的男子在不同场合闯红灯过马路。其中一半情况下，他身着熨烫笔挺的商务套装和领带；另一半情况下，他则穿着工作衬衫和长裤。研究人员在远处观察，并统计有多少在路口等候的行人跟随他过马路。就像哈默尔恩的孩童追随花衣魔笛手一样，跟随这位身着西装的“乱穿马路者”过马路的行人数量是之前的3.5倍。不过，在这种情况下，神奇之处并非来自他的魔笛，而是来自他那身条纹西装。

It is noteworthy that the two types of authority apparel shown by the above research to be influential—the guard uniform and business suit—are combined deftly by confidence men in a fraud called the bank-examiner scheme. The target of the swindle can be anyone, but elderly persons living alone are preferred. The con begins when a man dressed in a properly conservative three-piece business suit appears at the door of a likely victim. Everything about his clothing sends a message of propriety and respectability. The white shirt is starched; the wing-tip shoes glow deeply. His suit is not trendy but classic: The lapels are three inches wide—no more, no less; the cloth is heavy and substantial, even in July; the tones are muted, business blue, business gray, business black.

值得注意的是，上述研究表明，两种具有影响力的权威着装——保安制服和商务西装——被骗子巧妙地结合在一种名为“银行审查员骗局”的诈骗活动中。诈骗目标可以是任何人，但独居老人更受青睐。骗局始于一名身着保守得体的三件套商务西装的男子出现在潜在受害者的家门口。他衣着的每一个细节都传递着得体和体面的信息。白衬衫浆得笔挺；翼尖皮鞋锃亮。他的西装并非时髦款式，而是经典之作：翻领宽三英寸——不多不少；面料厚实厚重，即使在七月也是如此；色调沉稳，以商务蓝、商务灰和商务黑为主。

He explains to his intended victim—perhaps a widow he secretly followed home from the bank a day or tWo earlier—that he is a professional bank examiner who, in the course of auditing the books of her bank, has found some seeming irregularities. He thinks he has spotted the culprit, a bank officer who is regularly doctoring reports of transactions in certain accounts. He says that the widow's account may be one of these, but he can't be sure until he has hard evidence. Therefore, he has come to ask for her cooperation. Would she help out by withdrawing her savings so a team of examiners and responsible bank officials can trace the record of the transaction as it passes across the suspect's desk?

他向他的目标——或许是前一两天他偷偷跟踪从银行回家的那位寡妇——解释说，他是一名专业的银行审查员，在审计她所在银行的账目时，发现了一些疑似违规行为。他认为已经找到了罪魁祸首，一位经常篡改某些账户交易报告的银行职员。他说，这位寡妇的账户可能就是其中之一，但在掌握确凿证据之前，他无法确定。因此，他前来请求她的配合。她是否愿意帮忙取出自己的存款，以便审查员和相关银行官员能够追踪这笔交易的记录，看看它是如何经过嫌疑人的办公桌的？

Often the appearance and presentation of the "bank examiner" are so impressive that the victim never thinks to check on their validity with even a simple phone call. Instead, she drives to the bank, withdraws all her money, and returns home with it to wait with the "examiner" for word on the success of the trap. When the message comes, it is delivered by a uniformed bank guard, who arrives after closing hours to announce that all is well—apparently the widow's account was not one of those being tampered with. Greatly relieved, the "examiner" offers gracious thanks and, since the bank is now conveniently closed, instructs the guard to return the lady's money to the vault, to save her the trouble of doing so the next day. With smiles and handshakes all around, the guard takes the funds and leaves the "examiner" to express a few more minutes of thanks before he, too, exits. Naturally, as the victim eventually discovers, the "guard" is no more a guard than the "examiner" is an examiner. What they are is a pair of bunco artists who have recognized the capacity of carefully counterfeited uniforms to click us into mesmerized compliance with "authority."

“银行检查员”的外表和举止往往令人印象深刻，以至于受害者根本不会想到要核实他们的身份，哪怕只是打个电话。相反，她会开车去银行，取出所有积蓄，然后带着钱回家，和“检查员”一起等待陷阱成功的消息。消息到来时，是一位身穿制服的银行保安送来的，他会在银行关门后赶到，宣布一切正常——显然，这位寡妇的账户并没有被篡改。“检查员”如释重负，热情地表示感谢，并趁着银行已经关门，指示保安把女士的钱放回金库，免得她第二天再去取。大家面带微笑，握手道别，保安拿走了钱，留下“检查员”再道谢几分钟，然后也离开了。当然，正如受害者最终发现的那样，“保安”和“检查员”一样，根本就不是保安，也不是检查员。他们是一对骗子，他们意识到精心伪造的制服能够让我们对“权威”产生迷惑性的顺从。

Trappings

服饰

Aside from its function in uniforms, clothing can symbolize a more generalized type of authority when it serves an ornamental purpose. Finely styled and expensive clothes carry an aura of status and position, as do trappings such as jewelry and cars. The last of these status symbols is particularly interesting in the United States, where "the American love affair with the automobile" gives it unusual significance.

除了作为制服之外，服装在兼具装饰功能时，也能象征一种更广泛的权威。款式精美、价格昂贵的服饰，以及珠宝、汽车等配饰，都带有地位和身份的象征意义。在美国，汽车的地位象征尤为引人注目，因为美国人对汽车的“热爱”赋予了它特殊的意义。

According to the findings of a study done in the San Francisco Bay area, owners of prestige autos receive a special kind of deference from us. The experimenters discovered that motorists would wait significantly longer before honking their horns at a new, luxury car stopped in front of a green traffic light than at an older, economy model. The motorists had little patience with the economy-car driver: Nearly all sounded their horns, and the majority of these did so more than once; two simply rammed into his rear bumper. So intimidating was the aura of the prestige automobile, however, that 50 percent of the motorists waited respectfully behind it, never touching their horns, until it drove on.

根据旧金山湾区一项研究的发现，豪华车车主会受到我们特殊的尊重。实验人员发现，当一辆崭新的豪华车停在绿灯前时，其他司机鸣笛的等待时间明显长于对一辆老旧的经济型轿车。司机们对经济型轿车的司机几乎没有耐心：几乎所有人都鸣笛，其中大多数人还鸣笛不止一次；还有两位司机直接撞上了经济型轿车的后保险杠。然而，豪华车的气场如此强大，以至于有50%的司机恭敬地跟在它后面，始终没有按喇叭，直到它驶离。

Later on, the researchers asked college students what they would have done in such situations. Compared to the true findings of the experiment, the students consistently underestimated the time it would take them to honk at the luxury car. The male students were especially inaccurate, feeling that they would honk faster at the prestige- than the economy-car driver; of course, the study itself showed just the opposite. Note the similarity of this pattern to much other research on authority pressures. As in Milgram's research, the midwestern hospital-nurses' study, and the security-guard-uniform experiment, people were unable to predict correctly how they or others would react to authority influence. In each instance, the effect of such influence was grossly underestimated. This property of authority status may account for much of its success as a compliance device. Not only does it work forcefully on us, but it also does so unexpectedly.

之后，研究人员询问大学生们在类似情况下会怎么做。与实验的真实结果相比，学生们普遍低估了自己向豪华车鸣笛所需的时间。男生尤其不准确，他们认为自己会比向经济型轿车司机鸣笛更快；当然，研究结果恰恰相反。值得注意的是，这种模式与许多其他关于权威压力的研究结果相似。正如米尔格拉姆的研究、中西部医院护士实验以及保安制服实验一样，人们无法正确预测自己或他人对权威影响的反应。在每一种情况下，这种影响的效果都被严重低估了。权威地位的这种特性或许可以解释其作为一种服从手段的成功之处。它不仅对我们产生强大的作用，而且这种作用往往出乎意料。

HOW TO SAY NO

如何说“不”

One protective tactic we can use against authority status is to remove its element of surprise. Because we typically misperceive the profound impact of authority (and its symbols) on our actions, we are at the disadvantage of being insufficiently cautious about its presence in compliance situations. A fundamental form of defense against this problem, therefore, is a heightened awareness of authority power. When this awareness is coupled with a recognition of how easily authority symbols can be faked, the benefit will be a properly guarded approach to situations involving authority-influence attempts.

对抗权威地位的一种保护策略是消除其突袭性。由于我们通常会低估权威（及其象征）对我们行为的深远影响，因此在需要服从的情况下，我们往往对权威的存在不够警惕。因此，应对这一问题的基本防御手段是提高对权威力量的认知。当这种认知与对权威象征易于伪造的认识相结合时，就能在涉及权威影响的情境中采取更妥善的防范措施。

Sounds simple, right? And in a way it is. A better understanding of the workings of authority influence should help us resist it. Yet there is a perverse complication—the familiar one inherent in all weapons of influence: We shouldn't want to resist altogether, or even most of the time. Generally, authority figures know what they are talking about. Physicians, judges, corporate executives, legislative leaders, and the like have typically gained their positions because of superior knowledge and judgment. Thus, as a rule, their directives offer excellent counsel. The trick is to be able to recognize without much strain or vigilance when authority promptings are best followed and when they should be resisted.

听起来很简单，对吧？某种程度上确实如此。更好地理解权威影响的运作机制应该有助于我们抵制它。然而，这里存在一个棘手的问题——所有影响力手段都固有的这个常见问题：我们不应该完全抵制，甚至不应该总是抵制。通常，权威人士都知道自己在说什么。医生、法官、企业高管、立法领导人等等，通常都是凭借卓越的知识和判断力获得职位的。因此，一般来说，他们的指示都是很好的建议。关键在于，我们能否毫不费力或过度警惕地识别出何时应该听从权威的指示，何时应该抵制。

Posing two questions to ourselves can help enormously to accomplish this trick. The first is to ask, when we are confronted with what appears to be an authority figure's influence attempt, "Is this authority truly an expert?" The question is helpful because it focuses our attention on a pair of crucial pieces of information: the authority's credentials and the relevance of those credentials to the topic at hand. By orienting in this simple way toward the evidence for authority status, we can avoid the major pitfalls of automatic deference. An illustration or two is in order.

提出两个问题对掌握这个技巧大有裨益。第一个问题是，当我们面对看似权威人士试图施加影响的情况时，要问自己：“这位权威人士真的是专家吗？”这个问题很有帮助，因为它能让我们关注两个关键信息：权威人士的资历以及这些资历与当前主题的相关性。通过这种简单的方式，关注权威人士的资历，我们可以避免盲目服从的主要陷阱。下面举一两个例子。

Let's examine the highly successful Robert Young Sanka-coffee commercial in this light. If, rather than responding to his "Marcus Welby, M.D." association, people had focused on Mr. Young's actual status as an authority, I am confident that the commercial would not have had so long and productive a run. Obviously, Robert Young does not possess a physician's training or knowledge. We all know that. What he does possess, however, is a physician's title, "M.D." Now, clearly, it is an empty title, connected to him in our minds through the device of playacting. We all know that, too. But isn't it fascinating how, when we are whirring along, what is obvious often doesn't matter unless we pay specific attention to it?

让我们从这个角度来审视一下罗伯特·杨代言的、大获成功的Sanka咖啡广告。如果人们关注的不是他与“马库斯·韦尔比医生”的关联，而是杨先生作为权威的实际身份，我相信这则广告不会如此经久不衰、广受欢迎。显然，罗伯特·杨并不具备医生的训练或知识。这一点我们都清楚。然而，他确实拥有一个医生的头衔——“医学博士”。当然，这显然只是一个空洞的头衔，我们之所以会把他与医生联系起来，也是因为他扮演了某种角色。这一点我们也心知肚明。但是，当我们忙碌奔波时，那些显而易见的事物往往被我们忽略，除非我们刻意去关注，这难道不令人着迷吗？

That is why the "Is this authority truly an expert?" question can be so valuable: It brings our attention to the obvious. It channels us effortlessly away from a focus on possibly meaningless symbols to a consideration of genuine authority credentials. What's more, the question impels us to distinguish between relevant authorities and irrelevant authorities. And this is a distinction that is easy to forget when the push of authority pressure is combined with the rush of modern life. The Texas pedestrians who bustled into city traffic behind a business-suited jaywalker offer a prime example. Even if the man had been the business authority his clothes suggested he might be, he was unlikely to be a greater authority on crossing the street than other people, including those who followed him into traffic.

这就是为什么“这位权威人士真的是专家吗？”这个问题如此重要：它让我们注意到显而易见的事实。它能轻松地引导我们摆脱对可能毫无意义的符号的关注，转而考虑权威人士的真正资质。更重要的是，这个问题促使我们区分相关的权威人士和无关的权威人士。而当权威的压力与现代生活的快节奏交织在一起时，这种区分很容易被遗忘。德克萨斯州那些跟随一位身着西装的行人闯红灯而涌入车流的行人就是一个典型的例子。即使这位男士的穿着打扮暗示他是一位商业权威，他在过马路方面也不太可能比其他人更有权威，包括那些跟随他进入车流的人。

Still, they did follow, as if his label, "authority," overwhelmed the vital difference between relevant and irrelevant forms. Had they bothered to ask themselves whether he represented a true expert in the situation, someone whose actions reflected superior knowledge there, I expect the result would have been quite different. The same process applies to Robert Young, a man who is not without expertise. He has fashioned a long career with many achievements in a difficult business. But his skills and knowledge are as an actor, not a doctor. When, in viewing the famous coffee commercial, we focus on his true credentials, we will realize quickly that he should be no more believed than any other successful actor who claims that Sanka is healthy.

然而，他们还是追随了他，仿佛他身上的“权威”标签掩盖了相关性和不相关性之间的本质区别。如果他们肯花点时间问问自己，他是否真正代表了该领域的专家，他的行为是否体现了他在该领域的卓越知识，我想结果会截然不同。同样的道理也适用于罗伯特·杨，他并非没有专业知识。他在竞争激烈的演艺圈里取得了诸多成就，拥有漫长的职业生涯。但他的技能和知识在于表演，而非医学。当我们观看那支著名的咖啡广告，并关注他的真实身份时，我们会很快意识到，他和其他任何声称Sanka咖啡有益健康的成功演员一样，都不可信。

Suppose, though, we are confronted with an authority we determine is a relevant expert. Before submitting to authority influence, it would be wise to ask a second simple question: "How truthful can we expect the expert to be here?" Authorities, even the best informed, may not present their information honestly to us. Therefore we need to consider their trustworthiness in the situation. In fact, most of the time, we do. We allow ourselves to be much more swayed by experts who seem to be impartial than by those who have something to gain by convincing us; and this has been shown by research to be true around the world. 1 By wondering how an expert stands to benefit from our compliance, we give ourselves another safety net against undue and automatic influence. Even knowledgeable authorities in a field will not persuade us until we are satisfied that their messages represent the facts faithfully.

假设我们遇到一位我们认为相关的权威专家。在接受其影响之前，明智的做法是先问自己一个简单的问题：“我们能期望这位专家说多少真话？”即使是最博学的权威人士，也未必会如实向我们提供信息。因此，我们需要考虑他们在特定情况下的可信度。事实上，大多数时候，我们确实会这样做。我们更容易被那些看起来公正的专家所左右，而不是那些能从说服我们中获利的专家；世界各地的研究都证实了这一点。通过思考专家能从我们的顺从中得到什么好处，我们就能为自己设置另一道安全网，防止受到不当的、无意识的影响。即使是某个领域的权威人士，在我们确信他们所传达的信息真实反映事实之前，也不会轻易说服我们。

When asking ourselves about such a person's trustworthiness, we should keep in mind a little tactic compliance practitioners often use to assure us of their sincerity: They will seem to argue to a degree against their own interests. Correctly done, this can be a subtly effective device for proving their honesty. Perhaps they will mention a small shortcoming in their position or product ("Oh, the disadvantages of Benson & Hedges"). Invariably, though, the drawback will be a secondary one that is easily overcome by more significant advantages—"Listerine, the taste you hate three times a day"; "Avis: We're number two, but we try harder"; "L'Oreal, a bit more expensive and worth it." By establishing their basic truthfulness on minor issues, the compliance professionals who use this ploy can then be more believable when stressing the important aspects of their argument. 14

当我们质疑这类人的可信度时，应该记住合规从业人员常用的一个技巧，以确保他们的诚意：他们会看似在某种程度上与自身利益相悖。如果运用得当，这可以成为证明其诚实的一种巧妙有效的手段。他们或许会提及自身职位或产品的一些小缺点（“哦，本森·赫奇斯的缺点啊”）。然而，这些缺点通常只是次要的，很容易被更重要的优势所弥补——“李施德林漱口水，你一天三次都讨厌它的味道”；“安飞士：我们是第二名，但我们更努力”；“欧莱雅，价格稍贵，但物有所值”。通过在小问题上展现其基本的诚实，使用这种策略的合规专业人士在强调其论点的重要方面时，会更具说服力。

I have seen this approach used with devastating effect in a place that few of us recognize as a compliance setting: the restaurant. It is no secret that because of shamelessly low wages, servers in restaurants must supplement their earnings with tips. Leaving the sine qua non of good service aside, the most successful waiters and waitresses know certain tricks for increasing tips. They also know that the larger a customer's bill, the larger the amount of money likely to come to them in a standard gratuity. In these two regards, then—building the size of the customer's charge and building the percentage of that charge that is given as a tip—servers regularly act as compliance agents.

我曾在一家我们大多数人都不认为是合规场所的地方——餐厅——亲眼目睹过这种做法造成的毁灭性后果。众所周知，由于餐厅服务员的工资低得可怜，他们必须靠小费来补贴收入。撇开优质服务的必要条件不谈，最成功的服务员都懂得一些增加小费的技巧。他们也知道，顾客的账单金额越大，他们收到的小费也就越多。因此，在这两方面——提高顾客的消费金额和提高小费占账单金额的比例——服务员经常扮演着合规代理人的角色。

Hoping to find out how they operate, I applied for waiter openings at several fairly expensive restaurants. Without experience, though, the best I could do was to land a busboy job that, as things turned out, provided me a propitious vantage point from which to watch and analyze the action. Before long, I realized what the other employees already knew—that the most successful waiter in the place was Vincent, who somehow arranged for patrons to order more and tip higher than for anyone else; in fact, the other servers were not even close to him in weekly earnings.

为了弄清他们的运作模式，我应聘了几家档次较高的餐厅的服务员职位。但由于缺乏经验，我最终只能找到一份勤杂工的工作。不过，事后看来，这份工作却让我拥有了绝佳的观察和分析视角。很快，我就意识到了其他员工早已心知肚明的事实——餐厅里最成功的服务员是文森特，他似乎总能想方设法让顾客点更多菜，给更多小费；事实上，其他服务员的周收入根本无法与他相提并论。

So I began to linger in my duties around Vincent's tables to observe his style. I quickly learned that his style was to have no single style. He had a repertoire of them, each ready to be called on under the appropriate circumstances. When the customers were a family, he was effervescent—even slightly clownish—directing his remarks as often to the children as to the adults. With a young couple on a date, he became formal and a bit imperious in an attempt to intimidate the young man (to whom he spoke exclusively) into ordering and tipping lavishly. With an older, married couple, he retained the formality but dropped the superior air in favor of a respectful orientation to both members of the couple. Should the patron be dining alone, Vincent selected a friendly demeanor—cordial, conversational, and warm.

于是，我开始在文森特的餐桌旁徘徊，观察他的待客之道。我很快发现，他的风格并非一成不变，而是变化多端。他拥有一套独特的待客之道，随时准备在合适的场合施展。当顾客是一家人时，他会热情洋溢，甚至略带滑稽，与孩子们和大人都保持着亲切的交谈。如果是一对年轻情侣约会，他会变得正式而略带傲慢，试图让那位他只跟他说话的年轻男士点餐并慷慨地给小费。如果是一对年长的已婚夫妇，他依然保持着正式的态度，但摒弃了高高在上的姿态，转而对夫妇双方都表现出尊重。如果顾客独自用餐，文森特则会选择友好亲切的态度——热情、健谈、温暖。

But Vincent reserved the trick of seeming to argue against his own interests for large parties of eight to twelve people. Here his technique was veined with genius. When it was time for the first person, normally a lady, to order, he went into his act. No matter what she selected, Vincent reacted identically: His brow furrowed, his hand hovered above his order pad, and after looking quickly over his shoulder for the manager, he leaned conspiratorially toward the table to report for all to hear, "I'm afraid that is not as good tonight as it normally is. Might I recommend instead the_or the_?" (Here Vincent suggested a pair of menu items that were fifty cents or so less expensive than the dish the patron had selected initially.) "They are both excellent tonight."

但文森特把看似违背自身利益的伎俩留给了八到十二人的大聚餐。在这里，他的技巧可谓炉火纯青。通常情况下，当第一位客人（通常是女士）点餐时，他便开始施展这套伎俩。无论她点什么，文森特的反应都如出一辙：他眉头紧锁，手悬在点餐单上方，迅速回头寻找经理的身影，然后神秘兮兮地凑近餐桌，大声说道：“恐怕今晚这道菜不如往常那么好吃。我推荐您试试……或者……？”（文森特推荐的两道菜比客人最初选择的菜便宜五毛钱左右。）“这两道菜今晚都非常美味。”

With this single maneuver, Vincent engaged several important principles of influence. First, even those who did not take his suggestions felt that Vincent had done them a favor by offering valuable information to help them order. Everyone felt grateful, and consequently the rule for reciprocity would work in his favor when it came time to decide on his gratuity. But besides hiking the percentage of his tip, Vincent's maneuver also placed him in a favorable position to increase the size of the table's order. It established him as an authority on the current stores of the house; he clearly knew what was and wasn't good that night. Moreover—and this is where seeming to argue against his own interests came in—it proved him to be a trustworthy informant, because he recommended dishes that were slightly less expensive than originally ordered. Rather than trying to line his own pockets, he seemed to have the customers' best interests at heart.

文森特这一招就运用了几个重要的影响力原则。首先，即使那些没有采纳他建议的人也觉得文森特帮了他们一个忙，因为他提供了有用的信息来帮助他们点菜。每个人都心存感激，因此，在决定给多少小费时，互惠原则自然对他有利。除了提高小费比例之外，文森特的这一招也让他处于有利地位，可以增加这桌客人的点菜量。这让他成为了餐厅当晚的“专家”；他显然知道当晚哪些菜好吃，哪些菜不好吃。此外——这正是他看似违背自身利益之处——这证明了他是一个值得信赖的“线人”，因为他推荐的菜品比客人最初点的要便宜一些。他似乎并没有想着如何中饱私囊，而是真正为顾客着想。

To all appearances, he was at once knowledgeable and honest, a combination that gave him great credibility. And Vincent was quick to exploit the advantage of this credible image. When the party had finished giving their food orders, he would say, "Very well, and would you like me to suggest or select some wine to go with your meals?" As I watched the scene repeated almost nightly, there was a notable consistency to the customers' reactions—smiles, nods, and for the most part, general assent.

从表面上看，他既博学又诚实，这种特质让他极具信誉。文森特也很快利用了这种可信度。当客人点完菜后，他会说：“好的，请问您需要我推荐或挑选一些佐餐葡萄酒吗？” 我几乎每晚都会看到这一幕，顾客们的反应却出奇地一致——微笑、点头，而且大多表示同意。

Even from the distance of my vantage point, one could read their thoughts from their faces. "Sure," they seemed to say, "you know what's good here, and you're obviously on our side. Tell us what to get." Looking pleased, Vincent, who did know his vintages, would respond with some excellent (and costly) choices. He was similarly persuasive when it came time for dessert decisions. Patrons who otherwise would have passed up the dessert course or shared with a friend were swayed to partake fully by Vincent's rapturous descriptions of the Baked Alaska and chocolate mousse. Who, after all, is more believable than a demonstrated expert of proven sincerity?

即使隔着这么远的距离，也能从他们的脸上读懂他们的心思。“当然，”他们似乎在说，“你知道这里什么好，而且你显然是站在我们这边的。告诉我们点什么吧。” 文森特看起来很高兴，他确实了解葡萄酒的品质，并会给出一些绝佳（当然也很昂贵）的选择。到了点甜点的时候，他同样很有说服力。那些原本会放弃甜点或者和朋友分享的顾客，都被文森特对火焰冰淇淋和巧克力慕斯的热情描述所打动，纷纷点了自己喜欢的甜点。毕竟，还有谁比一位久经考验、真诚可靠的专家更令人信服呢？

By combining the factors of reciprocity and credible authority into a single, elegant maneuver, Vincent was able to inflate substantially both the percentage of his tip and the base charge on which it was figured. His proceeds from this trick were handsome, indeed. But notice that much of his profit came from an apparent lack of concern for personal profit. Seeming to argue against his financial interests served those interests extremely well.

文森特巧妙地将互惠和权威这两个因素结合起来，通过一个简单的操作，大幅提高了小费的比例和计算小费的基础费用。他靠这个伎俩赚得盆满钵满。但值得注意的是，他的大部分利润都来自于他对个人利益的漠视。表面上反对自己的经济利益，实际上却对他的利益大有裨益。

READER'S REPORT

读者报告

From a Young Businessman

一位年轻商人的自述

"About two years ago, I was trying to sell my old car because I'd already bought a new one. One day I passed a used-car lot with a sign reading, WE WILL SELL YOUR CAR FOR MORE. Just what I wanted, I thought; so I stopped in to talk with the owner. I told him I wanted to get about three thousand dollars for my old car, and he said he thought I should be asking for a lot more because it was worth at least thirty-five-hundred dollars. This came as a real surprise to me, because the way their consignment system worked, the larger my asking price for the car, the less money was left over for them to keep after they sold it to somebody. Therefore, by telling me to ask for more than three thousand dollars, they were cutting off their own profits. Just like your Vincent-the-waiter example, they were seeming to argue against their own interests so I'd see them as trustworthy authorities; but I didn't realize this until much later. Anyway, I went along with the owner's idea that my car was worth more than I'd first thought, and I set my asking price at thirty-five-hundred dollars.

大约两年前，我因为买了辆新车，所以想把旧车卖掉。有一天，我路过一家二手车行，看到一块牌子上写着：“我们会以更高的价格出售您的旧车”。我心想，这正是我想要的，于是就进去和老板聊了聊。我告诉他，我的旧车我想卖三千美元左右，他说我觉得我应该要价更高，因为它至少值三千五百美元。这让我很意外，因为他们的寄售模式是这样的：我的要价越高，他们卖给别人之后剩下的钱就越少。所以，他们让我要价超过三千美元，实际上是在削减自己的利润。就像你举的那个服务员文森特的例子一样，他们似乎在故意损害自己的利益，好让我觉得他们值得信赖；但我直到很久以后才意识到这一点。总之，我最终还是接受了老板的说法，认为我的车值更多钱。我最初的想法是，我的要价是三千五百美元。

"After they'd had my car on their lot for a couple of days, they called saying that someone was really interested in it, but that the price was a little too high. Would I be willing to drop my price by two hundred dollars to sell the car? Convinced that they had my interests at heart, I agreed. The next day they called back to say the the buyer's financing had fallen through and that he couldn't buy the car. In the next two weeks, I got two more calls from the dealership, each asking me to drop my price two hundred dollars to seal a sale to some customer. Both times I OK'd it because I still believed they were trustworthy. But each time, the alleged deal fell through. I was suspicious enough to call a friend whose family was in the car business. He said this was an old trick designed to get sellers like me to reduce their asking prices to super low levels, giving the dealership big profits when they finally sold the car.

“我的车在他们的停车场停了两天后，他们打电话来说有人对这辆车很感兴趣，但是价格有点高。问我愿不愿意降价两百美元把车卖出去。我当时觉得他们是真心为我好，就答应了。第二天他们又打电话来说买家的贷款出了问题，买不了车。接下来的两周，我又接到了这家车行的两次电话，每次都让我降价两百美元，好促成一笔交易。两次我都同意了，因为我仍然相信他们。但是每次所谓的交易都告吹了。我开始怀疑，就给一个家里做汽车生意的朋友打了电话。他说这是个老套路，故意让像我这样的卖家把要价降到很低，这样车行最终卖出去的时候就能赚一大笔钱。”

"So, I went over there and took my car. As I was leaving, they were still trying to persuade me to let them keep it because they had a 'hot prospect' who they were sure would buy it if I'd only knock off another two hundred dollars."

“于是，我就去了那里，把车开走了。我离开的时候，他们还在试图说服我把车留给他们，因为他们有个‘潜在客户’，他们确信如果我再降价200美元，那个人肯定会买下这辆车。”

Once again in a Reader's Report we can see the influence of the contrast principle combining with the principle of primary interest. In this case, after the thirty-five-hundred-dollar figure was set, each two-hundred-dollar nick seemed small by comparison.

在读者报告中，我们再次可以看到对比原则与主要关注点原则相结合的影响。在这种情况下，在确定了三千五百美元这个数字之后，每两百美元的损失相比之下就显得微不足道了。

# ↩

Chapter 7 - SCARCITY

第七章——稀缺性

The Rule of the Few

少数人统治

The way to love anything is to realize that it might be lost.
爱任何事物的前提是意识到它可能会失去。
—G. K. Chesterton
——G·K·切斯特顿

THE CITY OF MESA, ARIZONA, IS A SUBURB IN THE PHOENIX AREA where I live. Perhaps the most notable features of Mesa are its sizable Mormon population—next to that of Salt Lake City, the largest in the world—and a huge Mormon temple located on exquisitely kept grounds in the center of the city. Although I had appreciated the landscaping and architecture from a distance, I had never been interested enough in the temple to go inside until the day I read a newspaper article that told of a special inner sector of Mormon temples to which no one has access but faithful members of the Church. Even potential converts must not see it. There is one exception to the rule, however. For a few days immediately after a temple is newly constructed, nonmembers are allowed to tour the entire structure, including the otherwise restricted section.

我居住的亚利桑那州梅萨市是凤凰城郊区。梅萨最显著的特点或许是其庞大的摩门教徒群体——仅次于盐湖城，位居世界第二——以及位于市中心、维护得极其精美的宏伟摩门教圣殿。虽然我曾远远地欣赏过圣殿的园林景观和建筑，但直到有一天，我读到一篇报纸文章，讲述了摩门教圣殿中一个特殊的内部区域，只有教会的忠实信徒才能进入。即使是潜在的皈依者也不能参观。不过，这条规则也有例外。在新圣殿建成后的几天内，非信徒可以参观整座建筑，包括通常不对外开放的区域。

The newspaper story reported that the Mesa temple had recently been refurbished and that the renovations had been extensive enough to classify it as "new" by Church standards. Thus, for the next several days only, non-Mormon visitors could see the temple area traditionally banned to them. I remember quite well the effect of the article on me: I immediately resolved to take a tour. But when I phoned a friend to ask if he wanted to come along, I came to understand something that changed my decision just as quickly.

报纸报道说，梅萨圣殿最近进行了翻修，而且翻修规模之大，按照教会的标准，已经可以算作“新”圣殿了。因此，在接下来的几天里，非摩门教徒游客可以参观这片传统上禁止他们进入的圣殿区域。我清楚地记得这篇文章对我的影响：我立刻决定去参观。但是，当我打电话问一位朋友是否愿意同行时，我很快意识到了一些事情，这些事情也立刻改变了我的决定。

After declining the invitation, my friend wondered why I seemed so intent on a visit. I was forced to admit that, no, I had never been inclined toward the idea of a temple tour before, that I had no questions about the Mormon religion I wanted answered, that I had no general interest in the architecture of houses of worship, and that I expected to find nothing more spectacular or stirring than I might see at a number of other temples, churches, or cathedrals in the area. It became clear as I spoke that the special lure of the temple had a sole cause: If I did not experience the restricted sector shortly, I would never again have the chance. Something that, on its own merits, held little appeal for me had become decidedly more attractive merely because it would soon become unavailable.

拒绝邀请后，朋友纳闷我为何如此执着于参观。我不得不承认，我之前从未想过要去圣殿参观，我对摩门教并无任何疑问，对宗教场所的建筑也毫无兴趣，而且我并不指望在那里看到比附近其他圣殿、教堂或大教堂更壮观或更令人震撼的景象。随着我的讲述，圣殿的特殊吸引力也逐渐显露出来，原因只有一个：如果我不能尽快进入圣殿的封闭区域，以后恐怕就再也没有机会了。原本对我来说没什么吸引力的东西，仅仅因为即将失去，就变得格外诱人。

Since that encounter with the scarcity principle—that opportunities seem more valuable to us when their availability is limited—I have begun to notice its influence over a whole range of my actions. For instance, I routinely will interrupt an interesting face-to-face conversation to answer the ring of an unknown caller. In such a situation, the caller has a compelling feature that my face-to-face partner does not: potential unavailability. If I don't take the call, I might miss it (and the information it carries) for good. Never mind that the ongoing conversation may be highly engaging or important—much more than I could reasonably expect an average phone call to be. With each unanswered ring, the phone interaction becomes less retrievable. For that reason and for that moment, I want it more than the other.

自从我接触到稀缺性原则——即机会越有限，我们就越觉得它珍贵——之后，我开始注意到它对我的诸多行为产生的影响。例如，我经常会打断一场有趣的面对面谈话，去接听陌生来电。在这种情况下，来电者拥有一个我的谈话对象所不具备的吸引力：他可能随时无法接听。如果我不接电话，我可能就永远错过了这次谈话（以及它所包含的信息）。即便当时的谈话可能非常精彩或重要——远超我通常对普通电话的预期——我也毫不在意。每次电话铃声未响，这次通话就更难挽回。正因如此，在那一刻，我更渴望接听这个电话。

The idea of potential loss plays a large role in human decision making. In fact, people seem to be more motivated by the thought of losing something than by the thought of gaining something of equal value. For instance, homeowners told how much money they could lose from inadequate insulation are more likely to insulate their homes than those told how much money they could save. Similar results have been obtained by health researchers: Pamphlets urging young women to check for breast cancer through self-examinations are significantly more successful if they state their case in terms of what stands to be lost (e.g., "You can lose several potential health benefits by failing to spend only five minutes each month doing breast self-examination") rather than gained (e.g., "You can gain several potential health benefits by spending only five minutes each month doing breast self-examination").

潜在损失的概念在人类决策中扮演着重要角色。事实上，人们似乎更容易被失去某物的想法所激励，而不是被获得同等价值的东西的想法所激励。例如，如果房主被告知隔热不足会造成多少经济损失，他们就更有可能为房屋进行隔热，而不是被告知可以节省多少钱。健康研究人员也得到了类似的结果：如果宣传册上敦促年轻女性通过乳房自检来筛查乳腺癌，那么如果宣传册上强调的是可能失去的东西（例如，“如果您每月只花五分钟进行乳房自检，就会失去几项潜在的健康益处”），而不是强调可能获得的东西（例如，“如果您每月只花五分钟进行乳房自检，就会获得几项潜在的健康益处”），那么宣传册的效果会显著更好。

Collectors of everything from baseball cards to antiques are keenly aware of the influence of the scarcity principle in determining the worth of an item. As a rule, if it is rare or becoming rare, it is more valuable. Especially enlightening as to the importance of scarcity in the collectibles market is the phenomenon of the "precious mistake." Flawed items—a blurred stamp or a double-struck coin—are sometimes the most valued of all. Thus a stamp carrying a three-eyed likeness of George Washington is anatomically incorrect, aesthetically unappealing, and yet highly sought after. There is instructive irony here: Imperfections that would otherwise make for rubbish make for prized possessions when they bring along an abiding scarcity.

从棒球卡到古董，各种收藏品的收藏家都深谙稀缺性原则对物品价值的影响。通常来说，如果一件物品稀少或正在变得稀少，它的价值就会更高。在收藏品市场中，“珍贵瑕疵品”现象尤其能说明稀缺性的重要性。一些有瑕疵的物品——比如模糊的邮票或重铸的硬币——有时反而价值连城。例如，一枚印有三只眼睛的乔治·华盛顿头像的邮票，从解剖学角度来看是不正确的，从美学角度来看也不美观，但却备受追捧。这里存在着一种颇具讽刺意味的现象：原本会沦为垃圾的瑕疵，一旦具有持久的稀缺性，便会成为珍贵的收藏品。

With the scarcity principle operating so powerfully on the worth we assign things, it is natural that compliance professionals will do some related operating of their own. Probably the most straightforward use of the scarcity principle occurs in the "limited-number" tactic, when the customer is informed that a certain product is in short supply that cannot be guaranteed to last long. During the time I was researching compliance strategies by infiltrating various organizations, I saw the limited-number tactic employed repeatedly in a range of situations: "There aren't more than five convertibles with this engine left in the state. And when they're gone, that's it, 'cause we're not making 'em anymore." "This is one of only two unsold corner lots in the entire development. You wouldn't want the other one; it's got a nasty east-west exposure." "You may want to think seriously about buying more than one case today because production is backed way up and there's no telling when we'll get any more in."

由于稀缺性原则对我们赋予事物的价值有着如此强大的影响，合规专业人员自然也会运用一些相关的技巧。稀缺性原则最直接的应用或许就是“限量供应”策略，即告知客户某种产品供应短缺，无法保证长期供应。在我潜入不同组织研究合规策略期间，我反复看到“限量供应”策略在各种情况下被运用：“全州只剩下五辆搭载这种发动机的敞篷车了。卖完就没了，因为我们不再生产了。”“这是整个开发项目中仅剩的两块未售出的转角地块之一。您肯定不想买另一块；它东西朝向，采光很差。”“您今天最好认真考虑多买几箱，因为生产严重积压，我们无法确定何时才能补货。”

Sometimes the limited-number information was true, sometimes it was wholly false. But in each instance, the intent was to convince customers of an item's scarcity and thereby increase its immediate value in their eyes. I admit to developing a grudging admiration for the practitioners who made this simple device work in a multitude of ways and styles. I was most impressed, however, with a particular version that extended the basic approach to its logical extreme by selling a piece of merchandise at its scarcest point—when it seemingly could no longer be had. The tactic was played to perfection in one appliance store I investigated, where 30 to 50 percent of the stock was regularly listed as on sale. Suppose a couple in the store seemed from a distance to be moderately interested in a certain sale item. There are all sorts of cues that tip off such interest—closer-than-normal examination of the appliance, a casual look at any instruction booklets associated with the appliance, discussions held in front of the appliance, but no attempt to seek out a salesperson for further information. After observing the couple so engaged, a salesperson might approach and say, "I see you're interested in this model here, and I can understand why; it's a great machine at a great price. But, unfortunately, I sold it to another couple not more than twenty minutes ago. And, if I'm not mistaken, it was the last one we had."

有时，数量有限的信息是真的，有时则完全是假的。但无论哪种情况，其目的都是为了让顾客相信某件商品的稀缺性，从而提升其在他们眼中的即时价值。我承认，我对那些以各种方式和风格运用这种简单伎俩的从业者们产生了一种勉强的钦佩。然而，最令我印象深刻的是一种将这种基本方法发挥到极致的策略：在商品最稀缺的时候——看似已经绝版的时候——进行销售。在我调查的一家电器商店里，这种策略被运用得炉火纯青，那里30%到50%的库存商品经常标价促销。假设一对夫妇在店里，从远处看似乎对某件促销商品颇感兴趣。有很多迹象表明他们对此感兴趣——比平时更仔细地查看电器，随意翻阅电器附带的说明书，在电器前交谈，但却没有试图向销售人员寻求更多信息。看到这对情侣如此投入，销售员可能会走上前去说：“我看得出来你们对这款机器很感兴趣，我能理解；它性能卓越，价格也很实惠。但是，很遗憾，就在不到二十分钟前，我把它卖给了另一对情侣。而且，如果我没记错的话，那也是我们店里最后一台了。”

The customers' disappointment registers unmistakably. Because of its lost availability, the appliance jumps suddenly in attractiveness. Typically, one of the customers asks if there is any chance that an unsold model still exists in the store's back room, warehouse, or other location. "Well," the salesperson allows, "that is possible, and I'd be willing to check. But do I understand that this is the model you want and if I can get it for you at this price, you'll take it?" Therein lies the beauty of the technique. In accord with the scarcity principle, the customers are asked to commit to buying the appliance when it looks least available—and therefore most desirable. Many customers do agree to a purchase at this singularly vulnerable time. Thus, when the salesperson (invariably) returns with the news that an additional supply of the appliance has been found, it is also with a pen and sales contract in hand. The information that the desired model is in good supply may actually make some customers find it less attractive again. But by then, the business transaction has progressed too far for most people to renege. The purchase decision made and committed to publicly at an earlier, crucial point still holds. They buy.

顾客的失望之情溢于言表。由于缺货，这件电器突然变得格外诱人。通常，会有顾客询问商店的仓库、储藏室或其他地方是否还有未售出的型号。“嗯，”销售员回答，“有可能，我很乐意帮忙查找。但我理解您是想要这款，如果我能以这个价格帮您找到，您愿意购买吗？” 这正是这种销售技巧的精妙之处。它利用稀缺性原理，让顾客在电器看起来最难买到——因而也最令人向往的时候——做出购买承诺。许多顾客确实会在这个格外敏感的时刻同意购买。因此，当销售员（总是）回来告知顾客找到了额外的货源时，他手里也拿着笔和销售合同。得知心仪的型号货源充足，反而会让一些顾客对它失去兴趣。但到那时，交易已经进行到相当深入的阶段，大多数人已无法反悔。此前在关键时刻做出并公开承诺的购买决定仍然有效。他们最终还是购买了。

Related to the limited-number technique is the "deadline" tactic, in which some official time limit is placed on the customer's opportunity to get what the compliance professional is offering. Much like my experience with the Mormon temple's inner sanctum, people frequently find themselves doing what they wouldn't particularly care to do simply because the time to do so is shrinking. The adept merchandiser makes this tendency pay off by arranging and publicizing customer deadlines—witness the collage of such newspaper ads in Figure 7-3—that generate interest where none may have existed before. Concentrated instances of this approach often occur in movie advertising. In fact, I recently noticed that one theater owner, with remarkable singleness of purpose, had managed to invoke the scarcity principle three separate times in just five words that read, "Exclusive, limited engagement ends soon!"

与限量策略相关的是“截止日期”策略，即为客户获取合规专业人员所提供的产品或服务设定官方的时间限制。就像我在摩门教圣殿的经历一样，人们常常会发现自己不得不去做一些原本并不想做的事情，仅仅是因为时间紧迫。精明的营销人员会利用这种倾向，精心安排并宣传客户的截止日期——如图 7-3 中报纸广告的拼贴所示——从而激发原本可能不存在的兴趣。这种策略在电影广告中经常被集中运用。事实上，我最近注意到，一位影院老板目标明确，仅用五个字就三次运用了稀缺性原则：“独家限时放映即将结束！”

Swindled

被骗

By Peter Kerr

作者：彼得·克尔

New York Times

《纽约时报》

NEW YORK—Daniel Gulban doesn't remember how his life savings disappeared.

纽约——丹尼尔·古尔班记不清他的毕生积蓄是怎么消失的了。

He remembers the smooth voice of a salesman on the telephone. He remembers dreaming of a fortune in oil and silver futures. But to this day, the 81-year-old retired utility worker does not understand how swindlers convinced him to part with $18,000.

他记得电话那头推销员油滑的声音，记得自己曾梦想着靠石油和白银期货发大财。但直到今天，这位81岁的退休公用事业工人仍然不明白，骗子们究竟是如何让他掏出18000美元的。

"I just wanted to better my life in my waning days," said Gulban, a resident of Holder, Fla. "But when I found out the truth, I couldn't eat or sleep. I lost 30 pounds. I still can't believe I would do anything like that.”

“我只是想在生命的最后阶段改善自己的生活，”居住在佛罗里达州霍尔德的古尔班说，“但当我得知真相后，我吃不下饭，睡不着觉，瘦了30磅。我至今仍然无法相信自己会做出那样的事。”

Gulban was the victim of a what law enforcement officials call a "boiler-room operation,” a ruse that often involves dozens of fast-talking telephone salesmen crammed into a small room where they call thousands of customers each day. The companies snare hundreds of millions of dollars each year from unsuspecting customers, according to a U.S. Senate subcommittee on investigations, which issued a report on the subject last year.

古尔班是执法官员所称的“电话推销诈骗”的受害者。这种诈骗手法通常涉及数十名能说会道的电话推销员挤在一个小房间里，每天给成千上万的客户打电话。据美国参议院调查小组委员会去年发布的一份报告显示，这些公司每年从毫无戒心的客户那里骗取数亿美元。

"They use an impressive Wall Street address, lies and deception to get individuals to sink their money into various glamorous-sounding schemes,” said Robert Abrams, the New York State attorney general, who has pursued more than a dozen boiler-room cases in the past four years. "The victims are sometimes persuaded to invest the savings of a lifetime.”

“他们利用令人印象深刻的华尔街地址，通过谎言和欺骗手段，诱使人们将钱投入各种听起来很诱人的骗局，”纽约州总检察长罗伯特·艾布拉姆斯说道。他在过去四年里处理了十几起“电话推销诈骗”案件。“受害者有时会被说服，投入毕生积蓄。”

Orestes J. Mihaly, the New York assistant attorney general in charge of the bureau of investor protection and securities, said the companies often operate in three stages. First, Mihaly said, comes the "opening call,” in which a salesman identifies himself as representing a company with an impressive-sounding name and address. He will simply ask the potential customer to receive the company's literature.

纽约州负责投资者保护和证券事务的助理司法部长奥雷斯特斯·J·米哈利表示，这些公司通常分三个阶段运作。米哈利说，首先是“开场电话”，推销员会表明自己代表一家名称和地址听起来很唬人的公司，然后请求潜在客户索要公司宣传资料。

A second call involves a sales pitch, Mihaly said. The salesman first describes the great profits to be made and then tells the customer that it is no longer possible to invest. The third call gives the customer a chance to get in on the deal, he said, and is offered with a great deal of urgency.

米哈利说，第二次电话推销主要是兜售产品。推销员会先描述丰厚的利润，然后告诉客户投资已经不可能了。第三次电话则会给客户一个参与交易的机会，而且语气非常紧迫。

"The idea is to dangle a carrot in front of the buyer's face and then take it away,” Mihaly said. "The aim is to get someone to want to buy quickly, without thinking too much about it.” Sometimes, Mihaly said, the salesman will be out of breath on the third call and will tell the customer that he "just came off the trading floor.” Such tactics convinced Gulban to part with his life savings. In 1979, a stranger called him repeatedly and convinced Gulban to wire $1,756 to New York to purchase silver, Gulban said. After another series of telephone calls the salesman cajoled Gulban into wiring more than $6,000 for crude oil. He eventually wired an additional $9,740, but his profits never arrived.

“这招的诀窍就是先在买家面前晃晃胡萝卜，然后再把胡萝卜拿走，”米哈利说。“目的是让买家急于购买，不去深思熟虑。”米哈利说，有时候，推销员打到第三个电话就气喘吁吁，会告诉客户他“刚从交易大厅出来”。正是这种伎俩让古尔班掏出了毕生积蓄。古尔班说，1979年，一个陌生人反复给他打电话，说服他汇款1756美元到纽约购买白银。又经过几轮电话，推销员哄骗古尔班汇款6000多美元购买原油。他最终又汇了9740美元，但他的利润却从未到账。
